title: Show HN: Rat Race (After Dark, 1994), ported from 68k assembly to TypeScript
author: shijie
body: Ported to TypeScript from Motorola 68k assembly!All the rats' behaviors are true to spec: Their distractions (sniffing, turning around, grooming, stopping) are all frame accurate and occur in the same ratios as the original. The artwork and animation speeds were extracted from the old bitmaps and jump instructions and are (as close as I can get) to being frame accurate.Enhancements:I ran tens of thousands of simulations and fixed a few unfair advantages rats had if they were in the outside lane—they would lurch forward quickly around the turns resulting in a 43% win rate as opposed to the 33% random roll rate one would expect. Now it's within 0.5% for every training level and every lane.I also bumped the max rat count up to 8 possible rats, and added a "lane passing" animation. It looks hilarious to see two rats side by side in the same lane, gunning their way to the finish line. Gotta have fair rat races.I also added my own names for the rats, inspired by Berkeley Systems' naming scheme.Now we can all scream at our monitors urging Flamin' Furball to turn around and start waddling again like it's 1994.Github: https://github.com/heyitsjames/rat-race

title: Show HN: Totle, daily math puzzle game; Saturday puzzles have the fewest answers
author: zemelett
body: My oldest two kids are off to college and since leaving we've been playing the Wordle and 'sharing' our solutions with each other. It's been a fun way to stay connected with them, and it's become a bit of a challenge to see if we can beat each other's solutions. This got me thinking about other ways I could connect with them. The thing about the Wordle is that it doesn't take a large commitment of time, you can just pull it out when you've a few spare minutes. So I set out to build a game that would borrow from many of the themes that keep pulling us back to Wordle. What I created is called Tōtle which fits another one of our (okay my) favorite things; Dad jokes and puns (as it’s pronounced total).Here's how it works. You get five different numbers from a number pool 1 to 20, and a target from the remaining pool. Combine two at a time with + − × ÷, using all five numbers, every result a positive whole number, each puzzle always takes 4 moves. You get 3 rounds and 4 undos per round; a medal for fewest moves (perfect 4 = crown). There's a spoiler-free share card, like Wordle’s grid.The combinatorics math works out like this: C(20,5) (that's choose 5 from 20) × 15 possible target numbers = 232,560 possible puzzles. An interesting side quest: exhaustive search discovered that exactly 6 can’t be solved. They all are from the group of 6 numbers: 3, 7, 16, 17, 19, 20. If any one of those is chosen as the target the other 5 cannot make the target. I'm not sure if there are any interesting reasons or patterns.Every puzzle was sorted into 7 difficulty bands, by how many solutions each has, to provide a way to add increasing difficulty along the week. Sunday draws from the easiest 30%, Saturday from the hardest 3%, the game shows “harder than X% of puzzles” on the hardest days; Saturdays so far have been in the 98th–99th percentile of difficulty. 5 Saturdays were discovered to have exactly one answer (answer here means ways that only regroup or reorder the same moves count as one); the first is #68, Saturday, December 19, 2026.A few things I'd love to know from y'all:Difficulty: does the Sunday-to-Saturday curve feel right, and are Saturdays too hard? I've experimented with a mode that offers some help. But it's still under development.First-time play: was anything confusing, like dragging vs. tapping or how rounds work?Phones: How does it play on your phone vs your computer?

title: Show HN: Vork – headless 3D and VFX engine for agents
author: raviparikh
body: I made an agent-native 3d/vfx engine.Agents are good at making interesting scenes in Blender/Unreal/Nuke/etc. But these tools are fundamentally limited compared to what coding agents are capable of. Many simplifying assumptions are baked into these tools in order to fit human authoring methods.In vork, agents write the whole scene as code, including their own shaders, materials, cameras and physics, and vork renders it on the GPU. The core API fits in about 2,500 tokens.So, for example, almost every 3d engine assumes light moves in a straight line. Light near a black hole does not; so the best you can do in e.g. Blender is faking gravitational lensing. In vork, you can model it for real.If you want a camera lens that simulates a dragonfly's eye, or realistically-modeled Fata Morgana, this is also possible in vork.

Many simplifying assumptions are baked into these tools in order to fit human authoring methods.In vork, agents write the whole scene as code, including their own shaders, materials, cameras and physics, and vork renders it on the GPU. The core API fits in about 2,500 tokens.So, for example, almost every 3d engine assumes light moves in a straight line. Light near a black hole does not; so the best you can do in e.g. Blender is faking gravitational lensing. In vork, you can model it for real.If you want a camera lens that simulates a dragonfly's eye, or realistically-modeled Fata Morgana, this is also possible in vork.

title: Show HN: Brick Atlas: Explore 1000+ LEGO sets on one zoomable canvas
author: gasi
body:
Hello HN, I’m Daniel and I run ZoomHub, a small deep zoom image service.Most online catalogs look the same: There’s a grid of thumbnails, limited to about 20–50 items, filters that refresh the page when activated, and pagination buttons to go to page 22 of 128.
It has always bothered me that you can’t see the whole collection and every action makes you wait and lose context.I built Brick Atlas to show it doesn’t have to be that way: You can browse 1000+ LEGO sets by zooming in, selecting a set, seeing different angles (at full resolution) and in the sidebar, the set’s piece count, price, etc. You can read the whole instructions (on some sets) without ever seeing a page refresh or losing your place. On a slow connection, the image simply gradually becomes sharper. Once you are done, you can zoom out and see all sets again. Apply a price filter to find gift ideas under $50 or switch to Real size layout to see how big the sets are in real life compared to each other. Toggle Box vs Built to switch between the retail box and the assembled set. For collectors, I added the scatter view to plot sets by piece count vs price so you can find the best value sets. Every change in filters or layout animates gently so you never lose the thread.I’ve been obsessed with zooming for almost twenty years. I interned at Zoomorama and later worked on the (Microsoft Live Labs) Seadragon team, in case this looks familiar to you :)The idea to use zoom and image streaming could be applied to photo galleries, a museum catalog, other products, or even scientific images. I just happened to pick LEGO because I’m an AFOL (adult fan of LEGO), have been wanting to explore their catalog like this for years, and hope there are lots of you who do too.I published this as a static data set to S3 behind CloudFront (700k WebP tiles) for performance and render it using OpenZoom, my own WebGL deep zoom engine. The data comes from Brickset (thanks to Huw, the founder, for his blessing) and the images from LEGO (also via Brickset). I used my ‘free’ Anthropic API credits from Ultra plan to classify images into box vs built, to extract tags and colors, etc. using Claude Haiku and Sonnet (spend: ~$60.)I’d love to hear how it feels to explore, what you’d do differently, and what collection you’d like to see this used with :)

comments.text: I kept losing banked Codex resets because they expire instead of auto-activating. I expected Dota 2 bottle/rune behavior: if you do not drink the bottled Regeneration Rune before the timer, it activates itself. Codex just drops them.So I built Bottled Reset Rune, a small open-source macOS menu bar app. Each spare Codex reset is a Reset Rune in the bottle. title: Show HN: Agent-email-guard – agent tried to send 400 receipts, stopped at 5
author: Iammnhamza
body: Show HN: Agent-email-guard – agent tried to send 400 receipts, stopped at 5

comments.author: Iammnhamza
comments.text: Hi HN. I run AgentiSend, an email API for applications and AI agents. This is the part we pulled out and open-sourced (MIT).The failure it's for: an agent's send tool times out, the model retries, and each retry changes a word, so idempotency keys never match. In the demo, 400 attempts to send one customer the same receipt: 5 go out, 395 are refused. (The demo raises the threshold so you can see it; the default refuses the 4th.)It's blast-radius control, not a filter. Whatever the model decides: at most N emails per hour/day/month, M per minute, no near-repeats to the same inbox, a kill switch, and a hold for recipients you mark (e.g. anyone the agent hasn't emailed before) until a person approves.Three forms, strongest first:- a Claude Code PreToolUse hook (npx agent-email-guard hook install) that checks every email-sending tool call, whichever MCP server it goes to- an MCP proxy (npx agent-email-guard mcp --wrap ...) for Cursor, Codex, Claude Desktop- a library for Node, Python, PHP and Go that wraps nodemailer, SES, Resend, Postmark or SMTPThe four libraries are one spec plus 49 shared test vectors, so they print the same decisions. npx agent-email-guard test runs 12 runaway scenarios (a prompt-injected forward, the 400-receipt loop, a recipient sweep, a reply-all storm) against a reference policy and shows what got through.Limits, stated up front: the library runs in the agent's process, so an agent that edits its own tools can route around it. The hook and proxy sit outside the agent's code but guard one machine. None of them stops someone who holds your provider API key from calling the provider directly. Our paid API enforces the same policy server-side, which is the only place that last gap closes. That's the line between free and paid.I'd like to hear about loops it misses and sends it blocks that it shouldn't.

title: Show HN: Emma, a real-time AI video persona from Nuance Labs
author: cvanea
body: Hi HN! I'm Claudia, first employee and founding researcher at Nuance Labs. We're a research startup based in Seattle and have just released what we've been working on for the past 18 months.Emma, a conversational audio-visual AI that you can have a video call with in real time. It might be a little rough around the edges but we think it's better than anything else out there (we're biased, of course). You don't need to make an account and it works from the browser with mic and optionally camera.Emma is built on our full-duplex audio-visual system, Nuplex. We focused on naturalness over existing benchmarks as we found they didn't correlate well with what people actually like or how we speak face to face. We think being uniquely expressive is more important than an averaged-out face, for example. Our blog goes into more detail: https://research.nuancelabs.ai/A beta developer API is available at https://platform.nuancelabs.ai/. We're taking safety very seriously so she may prematurely end the call, in particular for the API, but we're working on tuning that.Personality, across all modalities, was the most important part for me. I've spent the longest speaking to her and I think she can be a lot of fun! I'd love for people to try it out and I look forward to hearing what you all think.Thank you!(Apologies for the double post, someone external posted our demo before we were ready, oops: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50429477)

title: Show HN: ApiClay – Turn a Website, Google Sheet or Database into a Paid API
author: apiclay
body: Hi HN, I’m a reverse engineer, and I’ve seen the same problem repeatedly: people need data, but the path from “I need this” to “my app, agent, or workflow can use it” is messy.Vibe coders want a working endpoint in minutes. Developers want clean docs, predictable JSON, and no surprise integration work. Businesses want to enrich lists, monitor changes, and safely expose internal data. AI agents need APIs they can discover and call reliably. Sometimes, the API simply doesn't exist.ApiClay makes that whole loop easier.You can search a catalogue of APIs and datasets, inspect them in a playground, and copy ready-to-run JavaScript, Python, or cURL snippets into your app. Each API has its own reference, pricing, trials, and usage terms, so you can see what you’re calling before you go live.But ApiClay is not just an API marketplace.If the API you need does not exist, you can create one with Website to API: give it a page, map the fields you care about, and publish a stable JSON endpoint. It works with static and JavaScript-heavy pages, and can return clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links.You can also turn what you already have into an API:* MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Google Sheets, Airtable, Excel/CSV, and HTTP services can become API endpoints.* Import an OpenAPI/Swagger file to get docs, a playground, and billing for an existing API.* Publish only the fields you choose, control access, set trials, plans, usage limits, and pricing.* Aggregate multiple providers into one tidy response for comparison-style products.For AI, ApiClay exposes an MCP endpoint so Claude, ChatGPT, or custom agents can search for an API, inspect it, and call it. The idea is simple: instead of an agent hallucinating a data source, it finds a real API and returns an answer backed by live data.There are also practical data tools beyond discovery:* Websets / enrichment: upload a list, enrich each row, set a spend cap, and export the result.* Monitors: watch an API or webpage and receive a signed webhook when something changes.* Cloud browser: automate a browser session for pages behind clicks or JavaScript rendering, then return the values your app needs.* Extraction: turn a page into clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links without maintaining your own scraper.For people publishing APIs, credentials stay encrypted on ApiClay and are not exposed to buyers; publishers control pricing, limits, trials, and access. For consumers, browsing and reading docs are free, while paid calls are charged per request and shown before use.*ApiClay is where you find the data API you need, build the one that is missing, let AI agents use it, and optionally sell it.*We’d love feedback from HN—especially from developers building data-heavy products, teams dealing with messy internal sources, and anyone experimenting with agent-driven workflows.

title: Show HN: Negs (Spektrafilm) brings spectral film simulations to the browser
author: haasisnoah
body:
Hi HN, I'm Noah. Negs runs spektrafilm, Andrea Volpato's physically based film simulation, in your browser (it's completely rewritten in Rust and using WebGPU). Drop in a photo (JPEG, PNG, TIFF or a RAW), pick a film and a print paper, and drag the sliders. The picture updates as you drag, and nothing is uploaded: it all runs on your machine.Try it: https://getnegs.com/try/Code (GPLv3): https://github.com/noahhaasis/negsThere are also native apps on the same engine: SwiftUI on macOS, GTK4 on Linux, and Windows.Spektrafilm (it started life as agx-emulsion) isn't a LUT or a preset. It simulates the whole analog chain, negative and then print, using only the manufacturers' published datasheets. Andrea's original write-up on discuss.pixls.us is worth reading in full: https://discuss.pixls.us/t/spectral-film-simulations-from-sc.... Roughly, it goes like this:- Your RGB image is turned back into a light spectrum and exposed onto the film's three dye layers through their published spectral sensitivity curves.
- Each layer builds up density along its characteristic curve. Datasheet curves are measured with densitometers that see all three dyes at once, so they're first separated into a curve for each layer.
- DIR couplers: where one layer develops a lot of density, it releases inhibitors that hold back development nearby, in the same layer and the ones next to it. This is where film's saturation and its edge sharpness come from.
- Grain is simulated per layer, with fast and slow sub-layers, as random silver halide particles that become dye clouds. It depends on the density at each spot instead of being laid over the image.
- Halation: light passes through the emulsion, bounces off the film base and exposes the red layer again (it's at the back), which gives the red glow around highlights.
- The negative's dye spectra are then projected through a virtual enlarger with Y/M filtration onto print paper, which has its own sensitivities and curves, and the print is scanned back to RGB.Because it's a model, the controls are physical: camera exposure, print exposure, enlarger filters, how much DIR coupling, grain particle size, halation strength. Push them too far and the image breaks the way film does, with colour crossovers when it's badly over- or underexposed. And you can experimentw with each control. There are about 50 stocks: Portra, Ektar, Gold, Pro 400H, Superia, Kodachrome, Velvia and Provia slide film, Aerochrome and some B&W (HP5, FP4...). There are 9 papers and print films too, such as Endura, Crystal Archive and Vision 2383. The paper choice has a huge impact on the final look.Negs implements the entire chain and is orders of magnitudes faster than the original python Spektrafilm implementation, so you can play around with sliders and get live feedback.Feedback is very welcome, especially from people who have actually shot these stocks: tell me which ones look wrong to you.

title: Show HN: Airgap-check – find what your AI app silently downloads offline
author: humanethq
body:
# humanethq/airgap-check

Audit AI repositories for offline (--network none) crashes, silent telemetry, and .env secret routing

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-08T21:55:28Z

## Languages

- Go
- Makefile
- Shell

## Top Contributors

- humanetresearch (1 contributions)

---

## README

# Humanet airgap-check

Find out what your AI app downloads, or tries to reach, when the network goes away.

airgap-check

Go 1.22+ License: MIT

## Why

A common assumption: point the LLM base URL at a local vLLM or Ollama instance and the app is ready for an offline network (an air-gapped VPC, a hospital or defense network, a container with no internet). In practice, many libraries fetch something on first use: tokenizer ranks, ONNX embedding weights, corpora, price maps, or telemetry. Offline, these calls either fail at first use or hang for tens of seconds on retry backoff.

None of this is a bug in those libraries. They download once and cache. It only becomes visible when the network is gone. airgap-check tries to surface it before you deploy.

## What it does

- **Static scan.** Reads manifests (`requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `package.json`, `Cargo.toml`), looks for code patterns (`nltk.download()`, `from_pretrained()`, `tiktoken.get_encoding()`, `whisper.load_model()`, `next/font/google`) and classifies `.env` keys. It reads key names only; secret values are never read or logged.
- **`--run`.** Runs your app in `docker run --rm --network none` with a DNS sinkhole and socket hooks, and logs every lookup and connection attempt.
- **`--fix`.** Prints Dockerfile lines (offline `ENV` flags and build-time pre-warming commands) that you can adapt for your own image.

Go standard library only. `--run` requires Docker.

## Install

```bash
# macOS and Linux
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/humanethq/airgap-check/main/install.sh | sh

# With Go 1.22+ (also works on Windows)
go install github.com/humanethq/airgap-check/cmd/airgap-check@latest

# From source
git clone https://github.com/humanethq/airgap-check.git
cd airgap-check && make build && ./bin/airgap-check --help
```

## Usage

```bash
# static scan
airgap-check /path/to/repo

# static scan plus a Dockerfile snippet
airgap-check --fix /path/to/repo

# run in a container with no network
airgap-check --run /path/to/repo

# use your own image and a smoke test that exercises your code paths
airgap-check --run --image my-app:latest --run-cmd "python3 -m pytest tests/smoke_test.py" /path/to/repo

# machine-readable output
airgap-check --json /path/to/repo
```

### Example `--fix` output (abridged)

Read this before applying it: if your app loads Hugging Face models, pre-warm them at build time before setting `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` and `TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1`. Without a warm cache the app fails at startup instead of hanging.

```dockerfile
# --- BEGIN AIR-GAP & TELEMETRY REMEDIATION ---
ENV DO_NOT_TRACK=1 \
    NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 \
    ANONYMIZED_TELEMETRY=False \
    CHROMA_TELEMETRY_IMPL=none \
    SCARF_NO_ANALYTICS=true \
    HF_HUB_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 \
    HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 \
    TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 \
    LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2=false \
    CREWAI_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true \
    OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true \
    STREAMLIT_BROWSER_GATHER_USAGE_STATS=false \
    XDG_CACHE_HOME=/app/.cache \
    TIKTOKEN_CACHE_DIR=/app/.cache/tiktoken \
    HF_HOME=/app/.cache/huggingface \
    NLTK_DATA=/app/.cache/nltk_data \
    PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/app/.cache/ms-playwright
RUN mkdir -p /app/.cache/tiktoken /app/.cache/huggingface /app/.cache/nltk_data /app/.cache/ms-playwright

# Pre-warm Python tiktoken encodings at build time
RUN TIKTOKEN_CACHE_DIR=/app/.cache/tiktoken python3 -c "import tiktoken; [tiktoken.get_encoding(e) for e in ('cl100k_base', 'o200k_base')]"

# Pre-warm ChromaDB's default ONNX embedding model at build time
RUN HOME=/app XDG_CACHE_HOME=/app/.cache python3 -c "from chromadb.utils.embedding_functions import ONNXMiniLM_L6_V2; ef = ONNXMiniLM_L6_V2(); ef(['airgap-warmup'])"
# --- END AIR-GAP & TELEMETRY REMEDIATION ---
```

## How `--run` works, and where it stops

`--run` starts a container with `--network none`, mounts your repository read-only, and mounts a small observer:

- A DNS sinkhole on `127.0.0.1:53/udp`. `/etc/resolv.conf` points to it, so lookups that go through the container's resolver are recorded and answered with `NXDOMAIN`.
- Python (`sitecustomize.py`) and Node (`node_preload.js`) hooks that record socket-level attempts.

Limits:

- We validated `--run` on Python and Node targets. Other runtimes should be caught if they use the system resolver, but we have not verified that.
- Traffic to hardcoded IP addresses, or DNS-over-HTTPS, skips the resolver and is not caught.
- Only the code paths you exercise are tested. Use `--run-cmd` to run a smoke test that covers the paths you care about.
- The sinkhole refuses immediately. In a real enclave, packets may be dropped instead, so hangs can be longer than the times below.

## Benchmark

We ran airgap-check on 20 open-source Python and TypeScript AI repositories in two phases. Phase 1 (10 repos) was used to find failure modes and tune the rules. Phase 2 (10 repos) is a held-out set: the rules were frozen at commit `8ce2f11` before we ran it.

These are probe-based tests: we did not start the applications themselves. Under `--network none`, we executed probe calls exercising the specific library functions flagged by the static scan (for example, `tiktoken.get_encoding('cl100k_base')` for `gpt-engineer`, ChromaDB collection creation and insertion for `mem0` and `vanna`, Hugging Face model resolution for `docling` and `quivr`, and a baseline probe for `chat-langchain`). Exact probe commands, upstream URLs, and commit SHAs are documented in `benchmark/REPOS.md`.

### What the libraries do offline

| Library / call | Behaviour with no network | Host it tries | Observed |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `fastembed` `TextEmbedding()` | Retries 3 times (3 s, 9 s, 27 s), then raises `ValueError: Could not load model` | `huggingface.co` | ~39 s |
| `huggingface_hub` `hf_hub_download()` | Retries metadata checks with backoff, then raises `LocalEntryNotFoundError` | `huggingface.co` | ~23.5 s |
| `chromadb` `collection.add()` | Default embedding function downloads the `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` ONNX model | `chroma-onnx-models.s3.amazonaws.com` | fails in under 1 s |
| `tiktoken` (Python) `get_encoding()` | Fetches the BPE rank file on first use | `openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net` | fails in under 1 s |
| `nltk` `nltk.download()` | Tries to fetch the index and corpus | `raw.githubusercontent.com` | fails in under 1 s |
| `playwright` `chromium.launch()` | Fails if the browser binary was not baked into the image | `playwright.azureedge.net` | fails in under 1 s |
| `litellm` | Fetches its model price map at startup unless `LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True` | `raw.githubusercontent.com` | fallback warning |
| `crewai`, `chromadb` | Background telemetry threads on startup unless disabled | `telemetry.crewai.com:4319`, `us.i.posthog.com` | background timeouts |

Times were measured in a container with no network and an immediately refusing DNS sinkhole (see limits above). Browser-side telemetry, such as `posthog-js` in a frontend bundle, is a separate case: server environment variables do not silence it, because the requests leave from the user's browser.

### Held-out results (10 repos, rules frozen)

| Repository | Probe result under `--network none` | TP | FP | FN |
| :--- | :--- | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| `gpt-engineer` | exit 1 (`tiktoken`) | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| `gpt-researcher` | exit 1 (`tiktoken`, `nltk`) | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| `llama_index` | exit 1 (`tiktoken`) | 8 | 0 | 2 |
| `mem0` | exit 1 (`chromadb` ONNX) | 6 | 0 | 0 |
| `vanna` | exit 1 (`chromadb` ONNX) | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| `quivr` | exit 1 (`huggingface.co`, ~23.5 s of retries) | 3 | 0 | 0 |
| `docling` | exit 1 (`huggingface.co`) | 3 | 1 | 2 |
| `litellm` | exit 1 (`raw.githubusercontent.com`) | 3 | 1 | 1 |
| `pydantic-ai` | exit 1 (`tiktoken`) | 3 | 2 | 0 |
| `chat-langchain` | exit 0, no asset downloads | – | 0 | 0 |

These are probe-based tests: we did not start the applications themselves. A “true positive” means the flagged library fetches something when its call runs offline; it does not prove the repository reaches that call in normal operation. Telemetry findings (for example langsmith, posthog or sentry in several repos) are not scored in the metrics below.

At component level: 35 true positives, 4 false positives, 5 false negatives. That is 89.7% precision and 87.5% recall. This is a small sample, so treat the numbers as rough. At repository level, all 9 repositories with first-use downloads were flagged, and `chat-langchain` was correctly flagged as clean.

False positives (all 4): `pyproject.toml` is scanned as text, so dev and test dependency groups (`playwright` in `docling`, `litellm`, `pydantic-ai`) and an optional extra named `posthog` triggered warnings. `package.json` is parsed, so its `devDependencies` are skipped.

False negatives (all 5): OCR weight downloaders (`easyocr`, `rapidocr`, `paddleocr`), `FlagEmbedding`, and LiteLLM's startup fetch of `model_prices_and_context_window.json` were not in the frozen rule table. `--run` is meant to catch this kind of miss, but only on the paths it exercises.

## Supported checks

| Category | Pattern | Host(s) | `--fix` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Runtime download | `tiktoken` (Python) | `openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net` | pre-warms `cl100k_base`, `o200k_base` |
| Runtime download | `chromadb` default embedder | `chroma-onnx-models.s3.amazonaws.com` | pre-warms `ONNXMiniLM_L6_V2` |
| Runtime download | `fastembed` | `huggingface.co`, `cdn-lfs.hf.co` | pre-warms the model cache |
| Runtime download | `sentence-transformers`, `transformers`, `from_pretrained()` | `huggingface.co`, `cdn-lfs.hf.co` | sets offline `ENV` flags; prints model snapshot template |
| Runtime download | `whisper.load_model()` | `openaipublic.azureedge.net` | pre-warms the checkpoint |
| Runtime download | `playwright` | `playwright.azureedge.net` | installs the browser into `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH` |
| Runtime download | `nltk.download()` | `raw.githubusercontent.com` | pre-downloads corpora into `NLTK_DATA` |
| Runtime download | `spacy.cli.download()` | `raw.githubusercontent.com` | installs the model wheel at build time |
| Runtime download | `torch.hub.load()` | `github.com`, `download.pytorch.org` | flagged only; pre-populate `TORCH_HOME` manually |
| Build-time download | `next/font/google` | `fonts.googleapis.com`, `fonts.gstatic.com` | flagged only; suggests `next/font/local` |
| Server telemetry | `chromadb`, `crewai`, `langsmith`, `scarf` | PostHog, `telemetry.crewai.com`, `api.smith.langchain.com`, `scarf.sh` | sets the matching disable flags |
| Browser telemetry | `posthog-js`, `@sentry/*` in frontend code | PostHog, Sentry | flagged only; disable the SDK in your frontend code |
| `.env` keys | `OPENAI_*`, `ANTHROPIC_*`, `GEMINI_*`, `STRIPE_*`, `JWT_*`, `CLOUDINARY_*`, `AWS_SECRET*` and others | n/a | flagged only; classifies key names and git tracking status |

## Design principles

- Secret values are never read, stored or logged. `.env` files are inspected for key names, non-empty presence, and `git ls-files` status.
- `--run` mounts your repository read-only.

airgap-check is not a security certification. It reports what it observed; a clean result does not prove that your application is safe to run in an isolated network.

## Contributing

Found a library that quietly phones home, or a false positive on your repo? Open an issue with the package name, the call, and the host it tries to reach, and we will add or fix the rule.

## About

Open-sourced by Humanet, which is also building Frame, an early-stage hosting platform.

## License

MIT

author: AlexFromTwelve
body:
Docs 
 简体中文 
 Search ⌘ K 
Advisory alpha · JavaScript and TypeScript test suites
 The missing layer of your test suite.
 A passing suite tells you the tests ran. Spirolo reads the whole suite, with its setup files and CI, and shows where a pass proves nothing. It never runs your tests.
 $ npm install -D spirolo@alpha Copy 
 $ npx spirolo check Copy 
Install and first run 
52 findings 
 styled-components · 395 ms 
748 findings across 11 open-source projects.
 53,372 tests read in about 16 seconds.
 weak tests 314 weak tests 
 missing guards 136 missing guards 
 skips nobody tracks 98 skips nobody tracks 
 duplicate tests 200 duplicate tests 
Project Tests Findings Read in 
 styled-components 3,845 52 395 ms 
 expo 12,649 156 4.5 s 
 gatsby 3,509 117 862 ms 
 material-ui 4,832 14 3.1 s 
 carbon 4,662 110 1.1 s 
 mantine 5,013 72 2.6 s 
 Replayed at real speed: full runs of the alpha, start to exit, median of seven on one Linux machine at pinned commits. Findings are advisory, not confirmed bugs. 
Agents write tests faster than anyone can check them
 An agent can add hundreds of tests in an afternoon, and they all come back green. A reviewer cannot read them all, and CI only reports that they passed. Verification has to keep up with the volume.
Super fast
 Keeps up with the volume
 Written in Rust. It read 53,372 tests across 11 projects, fast enough to run on every change, by every agent.
0 tests run
 Adds no load to CI
 It reads files, so it needs no browser, no database and no second test run. The 200 duplicate tests it found are time CI spends twice.
5 MCP tools
 Agents check their own tests
 An agent can call the same check while it writes, and fix a weak test before anyone reviews it.
136 missing guards
 Green means something again
 Setups with no guard against a console error or a leaked mock, so a test can pass when it should fail. When nobody reads every test, the merge gate has to hold.
New findings only
 Holds the line
 Ratchet once and CI fails only on what is new. No cleanup project first, and every new batch of tests meets the same bar.
Deterministic
 A second opinion that is not an LLM
 Same code, same report, every run. No model and no network: your code stays on your machine, and the tests are not checked by the same kind of tool that wrote them.
Five questions a green suite does not answer
 Every rule carries a public score; all 16 are on the rules page .
Weak tests 314 weak tests 
 Would this test notice if the code were wrong ?
hides the item count tag when itemCount is 0
 should stay closed when index is -1
 the day %s should be hidden
does not render an unvisited lazy tab
 should not display the previous button asserts only that DOM is absent 
hides the search input when hideSearch is true
search bar not rendered when options not provided
 non-custom leftItems render nothing in children
 should not populate textLabel prop when kind is not inline
does not render horizontal modifier when layout="vertical"
 when Link.Preview is not used, then does not render LinkNativeView, LinkNativePreview and LinkNativeTrigger

 should stay closed when index is -1
 the day %s should be hidden
does not render an unvisited lazy tab

hides the search input when hideSearch is true
search bar not rendered when options not provided
 non-custom leftItems render nothing in children
 should not populate textLabel prop when kind is not inline
does not render horizontal modifier when layout="vertical"
 when Link.Preview is not used, then does not render LinkNativeView, LinkNativePreview and LinkNativeTrigger
Merge gate 136 missing guards 
 Does a broken test actually block the merge ?
Unused tests 200 duplicate tests 
 Which tests add nothing the suite does not already check?
Flaky Experimental 
 Which tests can pass on one run and fail on the next ?
Health Experimental 
 Where does a new test pay first ?
C C grade 
 61 61 of 100
Health C (61) One number to watch, not to gate on
 Every report opens with a provisional health score out of 100. Each family takes off points for the share of its subjects that have findings, up to a cap per family, and rules outside the default view count half. It is a summary to watch over time: nothing gates on it, and the machine formats do not carry it.
 Reading a report 
Green is not the same as tested
 A passing suite rests on four layers. Most teams check the first and believe they have the rest. Two of them have no tool. Together they are the missing layer, and that is where Spirolo looks.
Mistakes inside a test file
 Checked by ESLint test plugins 
A test with no assertion, a focused test, an unawaited query.
The setup every test runs on
 Checked by Spirolo · no other tool checks it 
Whether a console error, a leaked mock or an unmatched request fails the test, or quietly lets it pass.
Whether the assertions catch a bug
 Checked by Stryker 
Mutation testing plants small bugs and reruns the suite to see whether a test notices. Thorough, and slow on a big suite: one run per planted bug.
How the tests connect to the code
 Checked by Spirolo · no other tool checks it 
Mocks that match no real export, absence checks with nothing proving the render happened, skips nobody tracks, gates that never gate.
This is an alpha. More rules are coming soon.
 No rule is proven yet, so the default view stays cautious: a rule shows only once at least 15 of its sampled findings were decided and at least 80% were true. The others still run, and --all shows them, labelled. How rules are measured .
spirolo check spirolo check --all 
 absence-anchor Weak tests advisory 16 / 20 
 fail-closed-setup Merge gate advisory 19 / 19 
 dead-skip Merge gate advisory 18 / 18 
 duplicate-test Unused tests advisory 15 / 18 
 12 rules run but are not shown: 4 experimental, 8 hidden. spirolo check --all shows them, each labelled.
Questions
What is Spirolo? Spirolo reads a JavaScript or TypeScript test suite with its configs, setup files, mocks and CI, and points at the tests that pass without proving anything. It is a native binary from npm, Apache 2.0 licensed, in advisory alpha. 
 Does it run my tests? No. It reads the files and never executes a test, so it needs no browser, database or network, only the project installed so imports resolve. It read 53,372 tests across 11 projects in 16 seconds on Linux x64. 
 How is it different from the ESLint test plugins? ESLint sees one file at a time, and most of the ways a suite lies sit between files: a setup that swallows console errors, a mock that matches no export, a skip nobody tracks. Keep ESLint for the inside of a file; Spirolo reads the wiring. 
 How is it different from mutation testing? Stryker plants small bugs and reruns the suite once per bug, which is thorough and slow on a big suite. Spirolo reads once and points at the structure that lets a bug through, and it can read a Stryker report to find tests that kill the same mutants. 
 Which suites does it read? Jest, Vitest and Playwright, with Testing Library, MSW and nock, on Linux and macOS (x64 and arm64). The rules are measured on React and plain Node or TypeScript projects; Cypress, Vue and Windows are outside the alpha. 
 What about false positives? A rule shows by default only once at least 15 of its sampled findings were decided and at least 80% were true, and that score is public. A wrong finding, reported with the file and the line, is how a rule gets better. 
 Can it fail my build? Not until you ask: every finding reports at info and the exit code stays 0. Give a rule warn or error in .spirolorc.jsonc, or run ratchet once so CI fails only on new findings. 
What would Spirolo find in your test suite?
 Your tests are the last check before production. In 11 popular open-source projects it found 748 findings, each project read in seconds. Install your project’s dependencies first, then run it from the root.
 $ npm install -D spirolo@alpha Copy 
 $ npx spirolo check Copy 
 Install and first run

title: Show HN: EtherPK Notes – An Agentic Kanban Board from Your Markdown Tasks [video]
author: gb2d_hn
body:
Author: Gareth Brown

EtherPK is at its core a markdown and Wikileakbased editor with rich functionality to help you manage information and projects. EtherPK tasks are plain markdown. But the EtherPK client has built powerful functionality on top of markdown tasks, integrating a cananban board, an MCP server to allow you to manage your work in your notes and easily hand off with instruction and full task context to your AI agent, for example, Claude Code. This demonstration shows you using the tasks you have added to your notes in EtherPK to hand off with context to an AI agent. Using EtherPK, the agent knows how and where to find task context, and you can even link to additional documents in your graph, making your graph an extension of the context available to the agent. The cards on this board are representations of task lines in plain markdown notes. Claude code is running in the terminal, and it's updating the markdown, which modifies the cards as it works. Here we see Claude code connected to a synced EtherPK graph. We show handing Claude code a task from the board and later a whole lane of tasks for autonomous working. A board shows the tasks that belong to one concept. Here the watering app page. It has six lanes, one for each task state, and each lane is split by priority. Drag a card to doing and the board writes the state into the task line. The board keeps no copy of the tasks, so a card moves whenever its line changes, whoever changed it. Select a card to open it in the task editor. The description is whatever is nested under the task, so it can hold links, pictures, and subtasks. This task has three subtasks and it links to the page with the watering schedule which the agent will need. Notes in a synced graph are encrypted before they reach the sync server. So the server has nothing an agent could read. The agent reaches the graph through the EtherPK headless client which runs on this computer and signs in as one of your devices. The steps are on the agents tab in settings. Create an agent setup code. Copy the login command and run it in a terminal. The code works once and expires after 10 minutes. EtherPK then asks you to approve a new device. Check that the code in the browser matches the code in the terminal. Approve it in EPK and press Y in the terminal. The second step tells the agent about this graph. Choose Claude code. Copy the command and run it. Claude Code can then use this graph from any folder. Inside Claude Code, the /mcp command shows the server connected with its tools. To hand over a task, select the copy button on its card. It copies an agent instruction, the graph's name, the task's words, a reference to the task, and which tools to use. Paste it into Claude code and say what you want done. The instruction tells the agent to change the task status only if it's asked to. So this request asks for that. The agent reads the task with read task, moves the card to doing, and reads the schedule page the task links to. The count on the card goes up as each subtask is ticked. Nobody is touching this browser. The changes reach it the same way an edit from another device does. When the tests pass, the card moves to test. The agent's note is in the tasks comments. It's an ordinary bullet under the task in the document, so you can edit it like anything else you wrote. Run the command to check the result, then drag the card to done. To hand over a whole lane, rightclick its header and choose copy agent instruction. The agent lists the lane when it reads the instruction. So tasks you move in after copying are included. This request is a triage against the goal written on the project page. The agent reads the page, sets the priorities, and the cards move into their sections. The headless client never holds the key to a protected document. An agent asking for one gets the same answer as for a name that doesn't exist. Low tool deletes a document, although an edit can empty one, and the agents token can't approve another device or delete a graph. The access tokens page lists it as agent on then the devices name. Revoke it there and that device loses sync access at once. The same steps work with codecs, cursor, and VS code. A local graph is simpler. It's a folder of markdown files. So the MCP server needs no signin. The steps are on the agents tab in settings and in the docs at docs.ek.com.

title: Show HN: Open-source app that lets LLMs control your iPhone (no Mac required)
author: ea016
body:
# EliotAndres/iphone-use-app An iPhone app where an LLM controls the phone it runs on - Stars: 4 - Forks: 0 - Watchers: 4 - Open issues: 0 - License: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 - Default branch: main - Created: 2026-10-19T14:05:48Z ## Languages - C - Rust - Shell - Swift ## Top Contributors - StephenDev0 (400 contributions) - neoarz (167 contributions) - CelloSerenity (83 contributions) - EliotAndres (69 contributions) - se2crid (40 contributions) - stossy11 (34 contributions) - hugeBlack (24 contributions) - jkcoxson (20 contributions) - wynwxst (19 contributions) - TreyHam27 (2 contributions) --- ## README # iphone-use-app **Let an AI model use your iPhone, from the iPhone itself. No Mac at run time (one-time pairing only), no extra hardware, no jailbreak.** iOS License: AGPL-3.0 Swift + Rust *Left: "Select a Lyft to the Eiffel Tower (don't book yet)" (4× speed): the agent leaves its own app, opens Lyft, types the destination, picks it and stops at the ride options. Middle: the finished run, each step with its screenshot. Right: a new chat.* ## Features - **No computer at run time:** the agent runs on the iPhone and controls that same iPhone, no extra hardware or jailbreak. A Mac is only needed once, to make the pairing file - **Start it from anywhere:** the chat, Siri, the "Run Agent" Shortcut or an `iphoneuse://run?prompt=…` link. ## Requirements | Part | Notes | |---|---| | **iPhone** | iOS 26 or later, Developer Mode on. | | **Apple account** | **Paid team:** the app uses its own built-in VPN (needs the Network Extension entitlement). **Free Apple ID:** build with `BUILTIN_VPN=NO` (Xcode build setting or `xcodebuild` argument) and install LocalDevVPN; re-sign every 7 days. | | **Pairing file** | Made once from a Mac over USB (below). | | **Vision model** | An OpenRouter key, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint whose model takes images and tool calls. | | **Mac with Xcode + rustup** | Only to build the app and make the pairing file. Not needed at run time. | ## Limitations - **Shortcut needed on cellular:** iOS refuses new loopback VPN connections on cellular data, so the app runs a Cellular Toggle shortcut that turns data off while it connects, then back on (or turn it off by hand). - **No other VPN at the same time:** it needs a loopback VPN (the built-in one, or LocalDevVPN), and iOS allows one VPN at a time, so Tailscale and similar stop while it is on. - **"Viewed remotely from Mac" notice on every run:** iOS shows "Device Hub: This device was viewed remotely from Mac" when its developer services are used, even though the "Mac" here is the app itself. Nothing leaves the phone (except calls to LLMs). - **Permissions:** requires Developer Mode, a VPN configuration, Local Network access (to find the phone's pairing service), and Location set to "Always" (keeps runs alive in the background, alongside silent audio). Microphone only for voice prompts. - **Pairing files expire:** make a new one when the app says so. - **Sideloaded build only:** it needs Developer Mode and developer services, so it can't go on the App Store. - **A few seconds per step:** most of it is the model. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph App["iphone-use-app"] L["LLM calling"] D["Mount developer image"] O["Orchestrator"] end L <-- "screenshot + history /
tool call" --> R["OpenRouter"] D -- "DDI mount" --> V["Loopback VPN
10.7.0.1"] O <-- "screenshot / tap, swipe, type" --> V ``` The app mounts a developer image, then uses a loopback VPN to screenshot and control the iPhone it runs on. Each step, the screenshot goes to the model, which answers with a tool call (tap, swipe, type, open app) until it's done. A Live Activity shows progress with a Stop button, and every run is saved as a chat. ## Quick start ### 1. Make a pairing file This is the one step that needs a Mac. There is no supported on-device API for the phone's developer services: the phone only opens them to a trusted host, the way it does for Xcode. The pairing file holds the keys of such a host, so the app can act as one for its own phone. Since iOS 17 these services are reached over a network tunnel (RemoteXPC/CoreDevice, the same path as Xcode's wireless debugging) rather than the USB mux, which is why the app can reach them through its loopback VPN with no cable. Plug the phone into the Mac, unlock it (tap Trust if asked), then: ```sh git clone https://github.com/jkcoxson/idevice && cd idevice cargo build --release -p idevice-tools --bin idevice-tools ./target/release/idevice-tools rppairing pair my-mac pairingFile.plist ``` The file keeps working until the phone stops trusting that host (Reset Location & Privacy, Developer Mode turned off). Make a new one if the app says the pairing file is invalid or expired. ### 2. Build and install the app ```sh scripts/build-idevice.sh # once: builds iPhoneUse/idevice/libidevice_ffi.a (needs the aarch64-apple-ios target) open iPhoneUse.xcodeproj # set your team, run the iPhoneUse scheme on the phone ``` ### 3. Set up (once, in the app) 1. Settings (gear, top right) → **Import Pairing File**. 1 2. Allow the **Add VPN Configuration** prompt. It only routes `10.7.0.1` back to the phone. With LocalDevVPN instead: turn it on, and pick LocalDevVPN in Settings → Phone Connection (picked for you if the built-in VPN fails). 3. Settings → **Model**: pick a provider, paste the key, pick a model. 4. Wait for the "not connected" line above the input to go away (the developer disk image downloads on first run). 1 Or copy it over once the app is installed: `xcrun devicectl device copy to --device --domain-type appDataContainer --domain-identifier blog.eliot.iphoneuse --source pairingFile.plist --destination Documents/pairingFile.plist` ### 4. Give it a task Type a goal, for example *"Open Settings and turn on Dark Mode"*, and send it. Stop it from the Dynamic Island or the chat. Development #### Scripted runs (no LLM) ```sh DEV= scripts/runscript.sh "open com.apple.Preferences; wait 1.5; tap 0.5 0.9; shot a" a ``` Launches the app with `-agentScript`, waits for "script done" in `Documents/agent.log` and pulls the screenshots. `-agentPrompt "..."` as a launch argument starts a real run. #### Simulator (layout checks only) The simulator can't reach a device, but it shows the UI. `-demoChat YES` plays a fake run (placeholder screenshots, a question to answer), Debug builds only. 1. `rustup target add aarch64-apple-ios-sim && scripts/build-idevice.sh sim`: the libs are single-arch, so the simulator needs its own, in `iPhoneUse/idevice/sim/`. 2. Build Debug (the scheme defaults to Release, which drops `-demoChat`) against that lib: `xcodebuild -project iPhoneUse.xcodeproj -scheme iPhoneUse -configuration Debug -destination id= LIBRARY_SEARCH_PATHS='$(PROJECT_DIR)/iPhoneUse/idevice/sim' build` 3. Install the `.app` from DerivedData and launch it with `-demoChat YES`. #### Heartbeat connection closes right after connecting (fixed: runs used to get killed) **Symptom (before the fix):** a run froze on a step after about a minute in the background, and the Live Activity stayed on that step. The app had been killed: the phone's crash logs held an `iPhoneUse.cpu_resource_fatal-*.ips` report ("exceeding limit of 80% cpu over 60 seconds", "Process killed"). **Cause:** the heartbeat thread (`Heartbeat.run()` in `DeviceSession.swift`) keeps CoreDevice services alive during a run. Its connection is closed right after the handshake; idevice's userspace TCP stack (jktcp) then answers every read with `BrokenPipe` in microseconds, and the loop retried with no delay, about 45k times a second. iOS kills background apps above 80% CPU over 60 seconds. Two things made it worse: - The idevice log was written to `Documents/idevice_log.txt` at Debug level, which prints every XPC message, screenshots included, as decimal byte lists: 178 MB of log and ~1 GB of memory in a minute. - The loop matched errors by the strings `HeartbeatTimeout` / `HeartbeatSleepyTime`, which never appear in idevice's messages ("heartbeat timeout", "device went to sleep"). **Fix:** timeouts are matched on the error code (100, sub-code 2) and the loop waits again; any other error ends the loop. The file log is at Info. **Still open:** why the heartbeat connection closes. Runs work without it (a 17-step, 2.5-minute run finished fine); if CoreDevice services start dropping on long runs, reconnecting the heartbeat (with backoff) is the next step. **Debugging a killed run:** `idevicecrashreport -u -k ` pulls the crash logs. Symbolicate with `atos` against the dSYM of the exact build (the UUID in the report must match `dwarfdump --uuid`). Feature scope: docs/FEATURES.md. ## Responsible use Only automate devices and accounts you own or may use, and respect the terms of the apps involved. The agent acts with your hands: watch it, and keep Stop within reach. ## Credits | Project | Repo | Used for | |---|---|---| | StikDebug, by Stephen and contributors | StikDebug/StikDebug | The tunnel, pairing file and developer disk image code is based on it | | idevice, by jkcoxson | jkcoxson/idevice | The Rust library behind every device call | | StosVPN, by the SideStore Team and Stossy11 | SideStore/StosVPN | The loopback VPN (`TunnelProvider/`) is based on it | | LocalDevVPN, by jkcoxson | jkcoxson/LocalDevVPN | The VPN app for free Apple IDs; our tunnel came from StosVPN through it | | esp32-iphone-agent, by Henry Yuan | onehumanbeing/esp32-iphone-agent | The model provider and model picker design, and the layout of this README | | DeveloperDiskImage, by doronz88 | doronz88/DeveloperDiskImage | Developer disk images | ## License AGPL-3.0. See `LICENSE`. # Aarv-1o/Attentry

title: Show HN: Attentry – a local checker that reviews each edit Claude Code makes
author: aarvsinghchauha
body:
# Aarv-1o/Attentry

to improve ai code

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-26T15:34:10Z

## Languages

- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- TypeScript

## Top Contributors

- Aarv-1o (137 contributions)
- claude (40 contributions)

---

## README

# Attentry

Attentry checks the code your AI agent writes. It works with Claude Code: after each edit, it
tells Claude about any security hole, crash risk, copied function or dead code that the edit added,
so Claude can fix it straight away. When the task is done, you get a short summary of what changed.

Website: attentry.js.org

Attentry is in preview. It reads JavaScript, TypeScript (including JSX and TSX), Python and Astro.

## Install

Install the extension from the VS Code Marketplace, or from
Open VSX if you use Cursor, Windsurf or another VS Code fork. Then open the Attentry panel in the sidebar and click **Connect Claude
Code**. That's all the setup there is. It adds Attentry to Claude Code for every project, and the
extension keeps it up to date.

## What Claude hears, and when

Attentry speaks up at a few moments during a Claude Code session, and stays quiet the rest of the
time. A clean edit gets no message at all.

- When a session starts, Claude gets one line saying Attentry is on.
- When you send a request, Claude is told about code in the repo that matches it, for example
 "the repo already has `timeAgo` in src/utils/time.js". That way it builds on what exists.
- When Claude finishes a plan, Attentry reads it and points out anything the repo already has: a
 helper the plan would write again, a route that already exists, a file that changes all the time,
 or a plan too big to do in one go. You can also ask for this check by typing `/attentry:plan`.
- Before an edit, if Claude is about to write a function the repo already has, it's told where the
 existing one is and how often it's used.
- After an edit, Claude hears about the problems that edit added, each one once. Problems that
 were in the repo before the task started are left out.
- Every 10 edits there's a short check-in, and your tests run in the background.
- At the end of the task you get a change card: the files Claude changed, the problems it added
 or fixed, and whether the tests passed.

By default Attentry only makes suggestions. In block mode it also refuses exact copies, and won't
let a task finish while it has added a security or crash problem. Switch modes in the panel.

### Tests

Attentry looks for your test command (`npm test`, `pnpm test`, pytest and so on, in each app of
the repo). You can set your own in `.attentry/config.json` with `"tests": "make check"`, or turn
tests off with `"tests": "off"`. A run is stopped after 300 seconds unless you change
`"testTimeoutSeconds"`.

Because a test command can run anything, Attentry only runs commands you've allowed. Connecting
Claude Code allows the current ones, and Attentry asks again if they change. `attentry doctor`
shows what's allowed.

### Tools Claude can call

Besides speaking up on its own, Attentry gives Claude four tools it can call when it wants to:

- `find_existing` looks for a function that already does a job, from a short description or from
 the code Claude is about to write.
- `check` lists the problems in Claude's changes, or in the files it names, and marks the ones this
 task added.
- `explain` gives the full story of the findings on one line: what the code does, why it matters,
 how to fix it and how to check the fix.
- `check_plan` runs the plan check on demand.

All four only read. They're built on the official MCP SDK and validate every call, so a bad call
comes back as an error Claude can read and correct.

## What it finds

**Security.** Routes with no login check, admin routes that don't check the role, records loaded
by id without checking who owns them, and logins with no rate limit. The same checks cover
Socket.io events, WebSocket messages, tRPC procedures, GraphQL resolvers and Next.js server
actions. In the code itself it looks for SQL, NoSQL and command injection, `eval`, SSRF, open
redirects, unsafe file paths, mass assignment, secrets written in the code, `.env` files in the
repo, XSS, CORS with credentials, leaked stack traces, weak password hashing, unverified JWTs and
`Math.random()` tokens. If your project uses a backend Attentry can't read yet (hapi or Elysia,
for example), it says so instead of reporting "no issues".

**Crash risks.** Async Express 4 handlers with no error handling, `JSON.parse` on data from
outside, and handlers that exit the process.

**Frontend and backend.** Calls to API routes that don't exist (with the route you probably
meant), calls with the wrong HTTP method, and routes nothing calls any more. It understands
Express, Koa, Hono, Fastify, NestJS, Next.js, FastAPI, Flask and Django on the backend, and fetch,
axios, apisauce, superagent, generated clients and Vite's proxy on the frontend.

**Database.** Money stored as floats, queries inside loops, trees fetched one level at a time, and
INSERTs without column names. It also flags `SELECT *`, `ORDER BY RAND()` and `LIKE '%x%'` as
hints. It works with Mongoose, Sequelize, TypeORM, Prisma, Knex, Django, SQLAlchemy, SQLModel and
raw SQL.

**Copies and dead code.** Exact and near copies of functions (showing what differs), including the
same logic written in both JavaScript and Python. Unused packages (with their size), unused files,
and functions nothing calls.

**Hotspots.** Complex files that change often, worked out from the git history, so you know where
a change is most likely to break something. This needs a git clone, not a downloaded zip.

**Code hygiene.** Errors that are ignored or only logged, commented-out code, comments that just
repeat the code, unused parameters and deep nesting.

To silence a finding, add a comment with a reason on its line or the line above:
`// attentry-ignore empty-catch: the cache is optional` (use `#` in Python). A comment without a
reason doesn't count.

## In the editor

The extension underlines problems in your changes, or in the whole repo if you click the status
bar. Hover over one to see what the code does, what can go wrong, and how to fix it. These
explanations come from the code itself, so they don't use any AI credits.

Security and crash problems show as errors, things that will break as warnings, and clean-up as
info. The light bulb can delete unused code (the only automatic fix), copy the fix so you can paste
it to your agent, or ignore the finding with a reason. If you mark more than 10% of a rule's
findings as not useful, that rule drops to a hint.

The Attentry panel shows what's wrong by category, whether Claude Code is connected, how its
current task is going, and when the repo was last checked.

The extension works in VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf and Antigravity. Other editors, such as JetBrains,
Zed and Neovim, can run `attentry lsp` as a language server.

## Command line

You need Node 22 or newer. From a clone of this repo:

```
npm install
npm run attentry -- scan path/to/your/repo
```

Useful options:

- `--changed` shows only what your branch or uncommitted work added.
- `--brief` prints at most ten lines, one per error or warning. This is the short version an agent
 needs.
- `--all` includes hints, the findings Attentry is less sure about.
- `--agent` prints each finding as steps an agent can follow.
- `--markdown` writes a report for a Markdown preview or a pull request comment. Add
 `--out attentry-report.md` to save it.
- `--json` prints the findings as JSON.

`attentry explain src/app.ts:42` explains the findings on one line, and `attentry doctor` checks
that Attentry is set up correctly and tells you how to fix anything that isn't.

To use Attentry with Claude Code without the extension, build it and set up the hooks in a repo:

```
npm run build
node dist/attentry.mjs init path/to/your/repo
```

## How it runs

Attentry runs on your machine and only reads your repo. Your code never leaves it.

A background process keeps the repo in memory, never on disk, so a check after an edit only
rereads what changed. That takes about 0.1 seconds on a 150-file repo and about 2 seconds on a
2,000-file one. The first read takes roughly 10 seconds per 1,000 files, and Claude doesn't wait
for it: edits made in the meantime are checked once it's done. The process stops after half an
hour without use.

The hooks, the tools and the editor all talk to the same process, so they always agree. If two
agents work in the same repo, each one only hears about its own edits. Every answer is signed with
a key stored in `~/.attentry` that only you can read, so nothing else can pretend to be Attentry.

## More

- SPEC.md: what version 1 will do
- AGENTS.md: rules for anyone, person or agent, working on this repo
- docs/research.md: the research behind the decisions
- docs/TESTING.md: how to test Attentry by hand

Attentry is open source under the MIT licence. Made by Aarv Singh Chauhan.

title: Show HN: MergeAtlas – A better way to review PRs
author: ismayilkarimli
body: Hey HN community, I built MergeAtlas - a better way to review PRs when bulk of the code is written by AI agents. It is a skill for your coding agent plus a small python script.MergeAtlas was built from a simple premise - When AI agents are writing the code, there's no need to review every single line of code. Instead it is better to understand the intent, important lines, and the blast radius.MergeAtlas helps you see the intents behind file changes, understand why each file was changed, and PR's scope all before you read a single line of code. When you are ready to read the code, MergeAtlas singles out the key lines from each file, so you are only focused on the most important lines.It goes further than GitHub's Files Changed tab as it also determines what files outside of the PR are affected by the changes.I tuned the skill till I was satisfied with the result in terms of structure, explanations, and verbosity.There's a live demo on the website based on an actual PR from excalidraw. Play around with it, and any feedback is welcome.Github: https://github.com/ismayilkarimli/MergeAtlas

title: Show HN: MeowDisplay Is iPhone Mirroring, but in Reverse
author: raiseCatError
body:
Hey HN and Cats, thank you for checking this out!Github:
https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplayEDIT 2: I should've mentioned that MeowDisplay started as a fork of OpenDisplay: https://github.com/peetzweg/opendisplay
which provided the foundational screen capture, virtual display, encoding and iPhone/iPad receivers. I've since taken it in a more phone-first direction, with work on the interaction, streaming and security layers. I've credited OpenDisplay and its developer Philip in the README under "Built on OpenDisplay".MeowDisplay is my take on the control your Mac from your phone scene. Available on iPhones, iPads and Macs, with Android rn in closed testing.The website has interactive illustrative demos if you'd like to see the app demonstrated.I think MeowDisplay does a few things differently, some of which I prefer and you might too.Such as Window view: allowing multiple tabs in split-screen type panes. Traditional Mirror/Extend views exist as alternatives. 
Floating windows: coming in the 2.1 release.Touch input approaches: Direct Touch(Classic or Natural), experimental Smart Touch, and Trackpad mode alongside Apple Pencil support. Doesn't sacrifice display space for a trackpad, use all of the phone's screen with your preferred mode.Stage Peek: shows a scrollable and searchable list of your Mac's windows on your phone along with an app drawer when you hold and pull on the left edge of your screen.It's free and open source so you can try it and see if it's for you without having to commit to it or anything.EDIT: I've used MeowDisplay during development whilst I was travelling between cities, left my acbook at home clamshell, powered, external display attached, and used it for small tasks remotely, it was pretty reliable even on a 5G network on a moving bus.Meow,
Jai

comments.author: raiseCatError
comments.text:
The question I saw coming, and was hoping for too.
Thank you for asking!There's quite a bit of overlap in what we're both trying to do. I've come across Sill and tried it as well, and it's nice.I think the biggest difference for most people would be the iPhone experience across both apps. I've specifically prioritized making the whole "use your Mac from your phone" experience better, and the iPad has received the same care too, with additional customizability to make use of the extra screen space.I've looked at quite a few remote desktop apps, how they've approached things and the trade-offs they've made, and weighed those against how I'd want MeowDisplay to do things.Part of MeowDisplay also came from a question: why hasn't Apple done something like this natively? The iPad has Sidecar, so I've often imagined how Apple might've approached it for the iPhone, and how I'd do it based on my experience with remote desktop apps.Coming to how they're different, I think the biggest distinctions are how I've chosen to handle Mac windows, the limited screen space on phones, and the overall UX.Sill's optional virtual display moves the selected window onto a separate display sized for the receiver, which can resize the actual Mac window. MeowDisplay's Window view keeps the Mac window's existing size and position, adapting how it's displayed on the phone instead.My reasoning behind this is that most desktop apps weren't designed for phone-sized windows. Resizing them can make their interfaces cramped or awkward, and I'd rather preserve their original layouts, even if that means occasionally zooming, which I find acceptable.Sill currently focuses on displaying one window or the desktop at a time, while MeowDisplay offers a different multitasking workflow with multiple windows arranged in tabs and panes, and floating windows coming in 2.1.Another difference is the screen space. Sill's portrait layout has the streamed picture at the top with a dedicated trackpad below it, although it also offers a Larger Picture option and direct touch.I've questioned why we even need a separate trackpad when the whole phone is already a touch surface. MeowDisplay lets you use the displayed content itself for Direct Touch or trackpad-style input, without sacrificing a portion of the screen for a dedicated trackpad. Personally, I find that screen space too valuable to give up.There's a difference in how you navigate through the UI as well. Sill has window thumbnails and app selection, while MeowDisplay uses Stage Peek, which you pull from the screen's edge to browse and search windows and apps, along with an expanded window overview.So yupp, we're both trying to solve a similar problem, just with different approaches and trade-offs. I think some people might prefer Sill's approach, and others might prefer MeowDisplay's.

comments.author: hbn
comments.text: Is there even a way to wake up a shut and sleeping MacBook? Or keep it awake at all? I'd be interested if there was that didn't have some caveat that will kill the battery.This seems more relevant than ever in days that we're sending off an LLM prompt and then letting it chug away for who knows how long. I tend to just leave my screen on with the mouse in a hotcorner that disables the screensaver.

comments.author: raiseCatError
comments.text: Nope! You do not need same Apple ID accounts or be on the same Wifi, it has AWDL for Apple devices and a similar equivalent for Android is being looked into.

comments.author: raiseCatError
comments.text: Similar idea, but not VNC. MeowDisplay uses its own streaming and control protocols, so you need the companion Mac app.I've considered supporting macOS's built-in Screen Sharing too, though with fewer features.

comments.author: raiseCatError
comments.text: There are ways to wake a sleeping Macbook, MeowDisplay has Wake & Connect, which uses Wake-on-LAN to wake a supported Mac on the local network, provided Wake for Network Access is enabled.It doesn't work for a fully shut-down Mac though, and remote waking over something like Tailscale isn't supported yet. That would need something already awake on the Mac's local network, like a compatible router or another device, to relay the wake request. I've been looking into that.As for keeping it awake, macOS already lets you prevent automatic sleep whilst you're plugged into power, even with the display turned off, so you wouldn't need to leave the screen running all the time.

extra.story_text:
Hey HN and Cats, thank you for checking this out!Github:
https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplayEDIT 2: I should've mentioned that MeowDisplay started as a fork of OpenDisplay: https://github.com/peetzweg/opendisplay
which provided the foundational screen capture, virtual display, encoding and iPhone/iPad receivers. I've since taken it in a more phone-first direction, with work on the interaction, streaming and security layers. I've credited OpenDisplay and its developer Philip in the README under "Built on OpenDisplay".MeowDisplay is my take on the control your Mac from your phone scene. Available on iPhones, iPads and Macs, with Android rn in closed testing.The website has interactive illustrative demos if you'd like to see the app demonstrated.I think MeowDisplay does a few things differently, some of which I prefer and you might too.Such as Window view: allowing multiple tabs in split-screen type panes. Traditional Mirror/Extend views exist as alternatives. 
Floating windows: coming in the 2.1 release.Touch input approaches: Direct Touch(Classic or Natural), experimental Smart Touch, and Trackpad mode alongside Apple Pencil support. Doesn't sacrifice display space for a trackpad, use all of the phone's screen with your preferred mode.Stage Peek: shows a scrollable and searchable list of your Mac's windows on your phone along with an app drawer when you hold and pull on the left edge of your screen.It's free and open source so you can try it and see if it's for you without having to commit to it or anything.EDIT: I've used MeowDisplay during development whilst I was travelling between cities, left my acbook at home clamshell, powered, external display attached, and used it for small tasks remotely, it was pretty reliable even on a 5G network on a moving bus.Meow,
Jai
