# ZeroPoint: a CPU-first, energy-based decision model

Picks the option that fits,

or says none does,

without being told that none is an option

 

 

ZeroPoint is a small energy-based model. It measures how well each option fits the text and compares it with a fixed level, zero, that stands for none of these. An option that fits no better than zero gets almost no probability, so ZeroPoint can answer none with confidence.

How to read the numbers. Half of the cases have no right option. A random guess, with none counted as one more option, gets about 13% right. Always answering none gets 50% on the first row and 0% when one option is right.

| | ZeroPoint | Strands Decider 2B ¹ | Clef-flash ² | Semantic Router | Zero-shot NLI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Accuracy: right answer, none included | 53.6% | 58.6% | 53.3% | 19.4% | 20.7% |
| Same answer whatever the order: decisions that change when the same options are listed in another order. Lower is better | 0% | 7.3% | 0% | 0.6% | 0% |
| Accuracy when one option is right | 43.8% | 58.4% | 56.2% | 38.9% | 41.3% |
| Silent mistakes: no option fits, yet it answers with ≥ 90% confidence. Lower is better | 7.8% | 0.0% | 5.8% | – ³ | 22.2% |
| Confident when right: right answers stated with ≥ 90% confidence. Higher is better, and it is what makes the row above comparable: a model that never states 90% cannot make a silent mistake | 66% | 37% | ⟨Clef⟩% | – ³ | ⟨NLI⟩% |
| Latency, median on a CPU (on a GPU) | 42 ms | 6,770 ms (93 ms)⁴ | + 20,000 ms (156 ms)⁵ | 17 ms | 1,697 ms |
| Model size | 89 MB | 4.8 GB | 19 GB | 91 MB | 369 MB |
| Runs on | CPU | GPU | GPU | CPU | CPU or GPU |

 Measured on the three tests no model is likely to have seen in training: a 2,000-case test and two support-ticket tests, 300 cases of each, 900 in all, half of them with no right option. ZeroPoint, Semantic Router and zero-shot NLI on a 2-core CPU with 2 threads, one case at a time. Semantic Router 1.1.1 with its default encoder; zero-shot NLI with DeBERTa-v3-base. ¹ AWS, Apache 2.0, and ² Cloudflare, Apache 2.0, each with "None of these" added to every list as one more option, so that it can answer none. ³ Semantic Router gives similarities, not probabilities. ⁴ On a CPU: measured on another 2-core CPU, on 118 cases of the 2,000-case test, where ZeroPoint takes 18 ms. On a GPU: an NVIDIA L4, on the 900 cases. ⁵ On a CPU: not measured, because Clef-flash needs about 19 GB of memory; a lower bound estimated from its size, 4.5 times that of Strands Decider. On a GPU: an NVIDIA L4, on the 900 cases. Per-test results, other confidence thresholds and the scripts to run it all again: BENCHMARK.md. 

Important

Hosted LLMs, through an API, are right in 57–60% of these cases, a few points more than ZeroPoint, and take 18 to 55 times longer. See the details here.

## ZeroPoint at a glance

| Size | Latency | Deterministic | Multilingual |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 89 MB, no GPU The model ships inside the package: nothing is downloaded at run time. Strands Decider needs 4.8 GB and a GPU; Clef-flash 19 GB. | 42 ms on a CPU Median on the tests above, on 2 CPU cores. On another 2-core CPU, ZeroPoint takes 18 ms per decision and Strands Decider 6.8 s. | Same input, same answer The order of the options never changes the decision; Strands Decider's changes in 7% of cases, and in 13% of support tickets whose own queue is not on the list. Same decisions on Linux, macOS and Windows, tested on every change. | 25 languages EU languages in the Latin script, plus Catalan, Basque and Galician. Which ones, and why. |

Routing a support ticket, finding the intent behind a request, sending a document to the right process: each means picking one option from a list. A classifier always picks something, even when the right option is not on the list or the text has nothing to do with the task. ZeroPoint can answer none, and the probability of none comes out of the same calculation as the probability of each option.

## Quick start

```
pip install zeropoint
```

```
from zeropoint import ZeroPoint

zp = ZeroPoint()
zp.decide("Can you move 200 euros from my savings to my checking account?",
          ["transfer", "balance", "pay bill"])
```

```
transfer  0.77  ███████████████·····
balance   0.02  ····················
pay bill  0.01  ····················
none      0.20  ████················
→ transfer · 12 ms

```

When none of the options fits, ZeroPoint says so:

```
zp.decide("Set an alarm for 6:30 tomorrow morning", ["transfer", "balance", "pay bill"])
```

```
pay bill  0.00  ····················
transfer  0.00  ····················
balance   0.00  ····················
none      1.00  ████████████████████
→ none · 12 ms

```

The options can be any short text, in any of the supported languages:

```
zp.decide("Me han cobrado dos veces la suscripción de marzo, ¿podéis devolverme el duplicado?",
          ["facturación", "soporte técnico", "recursos humanos"])
```

```
facturación       0.76  ███████████████·····
soporte técnico   0.00  ····················
recursos humanos  0.00  ····················
none              0.24  █████···············
→ facturación · 16 ms

```

See the Docs: javihaus.github.io/zeropoint.

## Integration

ZeroPoint runs in your process: one call per decision, no network, no GPU, no service to run. In a routing pipeline, gate on confidence: auto-route above your threshold and escalate the rest to human review.

```
d = zp.decide(text, ["transfer", "balance", "pay bill"])

if d.choice is None or d.confidence < 0.8:
    send_to_person(text)        # no option fits, or ZeroPoint is not sure enough
else:
    route(text, d.choice)       # e.g. "transfer"
```

The right threshold depends on what a wrong action costs you; pick it on a few hundred of your own labelled texts.

| Attribute | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `choice` | the chosen option, or `None` when none is the most probable answer |
| `confidence` | probability of `choice` (of none when `choice` is `None`) |
| `p_none` | probability that none of the options fits |
| `probabilities` | probability of each option, in the order you gave them; with `p_none` they add up to 1 |
| `depths` | how strongly the text belongs to each option (near 0: not at all) |
| `text_truncated` | `True` if the text was longer than ZeroPoint reads (192 word pieces) and its end was ignored |
| `options_truncated` | options longer than 16 word pieces, whose end was ignored |
| `blocks` | how many reads of 20 options the list needed |
| `latency_ms` | time the decision took |

Note

For many texts, `zp.decide_many(texts, options)` takes one list of options for all texts, or one list per text. Each text is computed on its own, so every result is exactly what `decide` gives for that text alone. Lists can be of any length. ZeroPoint reads the options in blocks of 20 together with the text, and every option's probability comes from one distribution over the whole list.

The option `ZeroPoint(threads=2)` sets how many CPU threads the encoder uses. The decisions do not depend on it.

## Calibration

You can calibrate ZeroPoint on your own labelled data, on a CPU.

```
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu   # optional: CPU-only PyTorch, without the GPU libraries
pip install "zeropoint[fit]"        # adds PyTorch and onnx; deciding never needs them
```

```
mine, report = zp.fit(texts, labels)   # labels: the right option for each text, or None for "none of these"
print(report["before"], report["after"])
mine.save("my-model")

zp = ZeroPoint("my-model")
```

Note

`fit` keeps 20% of your examples apart and reports how the model does on them before and after. Same data, same seed and same number of threads give the same model, bit for bit. On the support-ticket tests above, 300 labelled tickets raised the share of right queues from 24% to 36% when the queue is on the list, and from 29% to 46% against unrelated texts. Confident answers when the ticket's own queue is missing went from 20% to 0%. A fit is 200 steps and takes about 4 to 12 minutes on 2 CPU threads, depending on the CPU.

Warning

With few examples the held-out part is small, and the report's numbers move a lot by chance. `fit` and `recalibrate` warn when fewer than 50 examples are held out.

Tip

If your labels are already the ones ZeroPoint knows and you only want to move the balance between acting and answering none, `zp.recalibrate(texts, labels)` refits just two numbers, in seconds, without PyTorch.

## How it works

 

ZeroPoint is an energy-based model, in the sense of LeCun et al. (2006) ¹. It does not write an answer. It gives each option an energy: a number that measures how compatible the option is with the text, low when they fit and high when they do not. Training shapes these energies, pushing down the energy of the right option and pushing up the energy of the others. The text and all the options are read together, in one pass of a small multilingual encoder, so each option is measured against the text and against the other options.

Energies become probabilities with Boltzmann’s rule, the rule physics uses for a system in equilibrium: the lower the energy of a state, the more probable it is. A classifier applies the rule to the options alone, so one of them always wins, even when the text has nothing to do with any of them. ZeroPoint adds one more state, none of the options, with its energy fixed at zero: the flat ground around the wells the options form. Each option counts only by how far it falls below that ground. An option that does not fall below it gets nothing, however many such options there are, and none gets its probability in the same step as every option.

 ¹ Y. LeCun, S. Chopra, R. Hadsell, M. Ranzato and F. J. Huang, A Tutorial on Energy-Based Learning, in Predicting Structured Data, MIT Press, 2006. 

## Citation

```
@software{marin_zeropoint_2026,
  author = {Marín, Javier},
  title  = {ZeroPoint: a CPU-first, energy-based decision model},
  year   = {2026},
  url    = {https://github.com/Javihaus/zeropoint}
}
```

## License

ZeroPoint was trained only on data whose licence allows commercial use:

| Data | Licence |
| --- | --- |
| CLINC150 | CC BY 3.0 |
| Banking77, MASSIVE (English and Spanish) | CC BY 4.0 |
| Bitext customer support, banking, insurance and telco | CDLA-Sharing 1.0 |
| 5,000 examples written for this project | Apache 2.0 |

No data with a non-commercial licence was used for training, and none of the test texts above is in the training data. Details, with the criteria used to write the 5,000 examples, in docs/training-data.md.

The code is Apache 2.0. The model is built on multilingual-e5-small (MIT licence); the notices are in NOTICE.

## About

body:
# Dodaios/ste80-humanizer

STE80 Humanizer: agent skill that removes AI tells and rewrites text 80% of the way to ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English), the method Andrej Karpathy shared.

- Stars: 71
- Forks: 6
- Watchers: 71
- Open issues: 0
- License: Other
- Homepage: https://skills.sh/Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-09T17:18:59Z

## Languages

- Python

## Topics

- agent-skills
- ai-writing
- asd-ste100
- claude-code
- claude-skills
- codex
- cursor
- humanize-ai-text
- humanizer
- karpathy
- llm
- plain-language
- simplified-technical-english
- writing

## Top Contributors

- rubenluetke10-beep (5 contributions)

---

## README

# STE80 Humanizer

skills.sh installs validate License: MIT

STE80 Humanizer makes AI-written text read like a careful person wrote it, without changing what it says. It combines two methods:

1. **The humanizer method.** Remove the 26 tells from Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing, in the catalog of blader/humanizer.
2. **Karpathy's STE80 method.** Rebuild the sentences "80% of the way to ASD-STE100", the controlled English of aircraft maintenance manuals.

**Before:**
> Great question! Kubernetes liveness probes are a powerful mechanism that enables the kubelet to determine whether a container is healthy — and it's not just a health check, it's your first line of defense. When a probe fails, the container will be automatically restarted by the kubelet, ensuring that your application remains available. However, it's important to note that misconfigured probes could potentially cause cascading restarts, so parameters like `initialDelaySeconds` and `failureThreshold` should be carefully tuned.
>
> Get this right, and your cluster heals itself.

**After:**
> A liveness probe tells the kubelet if a container is healthy. If the probe fails, the kubelet restarts the container. This keeps the application available.
>
> A bad probe can also cause many restarts. For example, a timeout that is too short makes healthy containers fail the probe. To prevent this, set `initialDelaySeconds` and `failureThreshold` to values that fit your application.

The goal is text that people read easily. Getting past AI detectors is not a goal.

## Why two passes

Most humanizers only remove phrases. The text loses "Great question!" and "seamless", but it keeps long sentences that carry three ideas, hide the actor and stack hedges. It still reads like AI. You can see it in the worked example in SKILL.md:

| Step | What is left |
|---|---|
| Original | Chatbot opener, dash, "not just X", "-ing" rider, "however", "could potentially", dramatic closer |
| After Pass 1 (tells) | "...the container will be automatically restarted by the kubelet, which keeps your application available. Misconfigured probes can cause cascading restarts, so parameters ... should be carefully tuned." Clean words, but heavy sentences. |
| After Pass 2 (STE80) | Short sentences, one idea each, active voice, the instruction apart from the description. |

## The method: what Karpathy said

On 2 October 2026, Andrej Karpathy posted tips for one problem: as LLMs do more of the work, people spend more time reading and understanding what the models produce. His first tip:

> Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent.

The post then goes up a ladder: diagrams, then HTML pages, then explainer videos. His conclusion is that our work moves "up the abstractions into oversight and understanding". Clear output is the bottleneck, and writing is the first step.

Simplified Technical English: overview. Document structure, anatomy of STE sentences, verb forms, dictionary entries, writing rule limits and history.

*The STE overview graphic from Karpathy's post. Click to enlarge. Note: a later fact check found errors in the dictionary panel (D). In ASD-STE100 Issue 9, "approximately" is approved, "TEST" is approved only as a noun (not as a verb), and there is no entry for "in order to". This skill follows Issue 9.*

**ASD-STE100** (Simplified Technical English) is from the 1980s aerospace industry. It was made for mechanics whose first language is not English, because a misread step on an aircraft can kill. Its rules:

- 20 words per instruction and 25 per description
- one instruction per sentence
- active voice and simple tenses
- one meaning per word, with about 900 approved words
- one topic per paragraph, and six sentences at most

**Why "80%"?** At 100%, "check" and "test" are nouns only, "may" and "should" are banned and many common words are not allowed. Normal prose sounds stiff. At 80%, you keep the full structure and only as much vocabulary as still sounds natural:

| STE rule | 100% (Strict mode) | 80% (default) |
|---|---|---|
| Sentence length 20 / 25 | Hard limit | A few words over is fine |
| One idea per sentence | Always | Always |
| Active voice, simple tenses | Always | Always |
| Approved dictionary only | Yes | No, use the plain common word |
| "check", "test" as verbs | No | Yes |
| "may", "should" | No | Yes, for real uncertainty |
| Contractions | No | Yes, in casual text |
| Semicolons | No | No |

Karpathy talks about readability, not about sounding human. This skill adds that part, because the two methods cover each other's gaps.

## How to read the skill

SKILL.md has two numbered lists:

- **§1 to §26:** the AI tells (Pass 1).
- **S1 to S15:** the STE80 structure rules (Pass 2).

Every entry has the same fields: **Watch for**, **Problem**, **Before** and **After**. Pass 2 entries also say what changes between **80%** and **Strict**. *Weak alone* means: act only if other tells are near. The skill reports its edits by number, for example "§1, §8, S2", so you can look each one up.

## Installation

Once installed, the skill answers to `/ste80-humanizer`. It also starts by itself when you ask to humanize, simplify or de-AI a text, or ask for STE.

### Any agent (skills.sh)

```bash
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
```

Global install for one agent, or for all of them:

```bash
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent claude-code
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent codex
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent cursor
npx skills add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer --global --agent '*'
```

Without `--global`, the skill goes into the current project only. The skills CLI from Vercel works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and many more agents.

### Claude Code plugin

```
/plugin marketplace add Dodaios/ste80-humanizer
/plugin install ste80-humanizer@ste80-humanizer
```

### Claude.ai and Claude Desktop

Download this repo as a ZIP (Code → Download ZIP). Upload it in Settings → Capabilities → Skills.

## Usage

```
/ste80-humanizer
<paste text>
```

Or just ask:

```
This sounds like ChatGPT wrote it. Make it sound like a person.
Rewrite this README 80% of the way to ASD-STE100.
Explain how TLS handshakes work in STE.
Light touch: just remove the AI stuff from docs/intro.md.
Convert docs/runbook.md to strict STE.
Does this email sound like AI? Just tell me, don't rewrite it.
```

| Mode | When | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Humanize (default)** | Normal requests | Pass 1 fully, Pass 2 at 80%. Keeps your voice. |
| **Light** | "light touch", "just remove the AI stuff" | Pass 1, plus only the worst sentences from Pass 2. |
| **Strict STE** | "strict", "full STE", procedures, safety notes | Pass 1 and all of Pass 2 at 100%. |

**Match your voice.** Add a sample of your own writing. The skill then matches your sentence length, words and punctuation.

**Fidelity first.** The skill keeps every fact, keeps "may" as "may", keeps "40+" as "40+", adds nothing and flags contradictions in the source. In our tests, this was the clearest difference from a plain prompt (see Tests).

## Pass 1: the 26 AI tells

| # | Tell | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Staging instead of stating** ||||
| 1 | **Not X but Y** | It's not just a faster build tool, it's a new way to think. | The build tool caches each step. |
| 2 | **One-line closers** | ...No cold starts. No excuses. That's the power of the edge. | Latency dropped to 40 ms. |
| 3 | **Sayings that sound deep** | At its core, observability is the language of trust. | Shared dashboards show both teams the same data. |
| 4 | **Staged run-up** | Let's dive in. Here's what you need to know. | The API allows 100 requests per minute. |
| 5 | **Arguing with no one** | To be clear, I'm not saying microservices are bad... | We split the billing service out first. |
| **B. Rhythm by rule** ||||
| 6 | **Forced triads** | fast, intuitive, and powerful | loads in under a second |
| 7 | **Repeated openings** (*weak alone*) | It reads... It checks... It starts... | It reads the config and checks the schema. |
| 8 | **Dashes everywhere** | The migration — which took six weeks — is done. | The migration took six weeks and is done. |
| 9 | **Stacked qualifiers** (*weak alone*) | could potentially possibly cause | can break |
| 10 | **Hyphenated pairs** (*weak alone*) | The API is well-documented. | The API is well documented. |
| 11 | **Passive, missing subjects** (*weak alone*) | No account needed. | You do not need an account. |
| **C. Inflation and borrowed authority** ||||
| 12 | **Overused AI words** | leverages a robust caching layer, showcasing... | caches API responses on the device |
| 13 | **Inflated significance** | marks a pivotal moment in the project's journey | adds a CLI and drops Node 16 |
| 14 | **Vague association** | The outage was linked to the DNS change. | The DNS change caused the outage. |
| 15 | **Shallow -ing riders** | ..., highlighting its commitment to accessibility | (cut) |
| 16 | **Sales language** | our groundbreaking, world-class editor | The editor runs inside VS Code. |
| 17 | **Borrowed authority** | Experts agree... featured in TechCrunch, Wired... | It was on the front page of Hacker News in May. |
| 18 | **Avoiding is / has** | serves as the central hub and boasts 40 options | holds the settings. It has 40 options. |
| **D. Formatting by rule** ||||
| 19 | **Bold as decoration** | **Performance:** Performance has been improved. | The release makes pages load faster. |
| 20 | **Decorative headings** | ## 🚀 Getting Started With The CLI → | ## Install the CLI |
| 21 | **Curly quotes** (*weak alone*) | “true” | "true" |
| **E. Leftovers from the chat and the draft** ||||
| 22 | **Chatbot residue** | Great question! ... I hope this helps! | (cut the wrapper) |
| 23 | **Knowledge-limit hedges** | While details are limited, it was likely created around 2015. | The sources do not say. |
| 24 | **Heading repeated** | ## Security / Security is important. | (cut the line) |
| 25 | **Writing about the document** | This function was added to replace the old approach... | This function looks up users in a hash map. |
| **F. Writing for the wrong reader** ||||
| 26 | **Re-explaining what the reader knows** | A reply that walks through the whole diagnosis first | Agreed. I'll switch the job to UTC. |

## Pass 2: the 15 STE80 rules

| # | Rule | 80% vs Strict |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | One idea per sentence | 80% allows two linked facts with "and" or "because" |
| S2 | Short sentences: 20 words (instructions), 25 (descriptions) | 80% allows a small overrun |
| S3 | Condition first: "If X, do Y." | Same |
| S4 | Do not drop words ("the", "a", "that") | 80% allows fragments in tables and headings |
| S5 | Lists for steps and complex content | Same |
| S6 | Active voice | Same |
| S7 | Simple tenses only | Same |
| S8 | Verbs, not nouns, no "-ing" chains | Strict: "check" and "test" are nouns |
| S9 | Honest modals: can, must, will | 80% keeps "may" and "should" for real doubt |
| S10 | Plain words, one meaning each, no phrasal verbs | 80% keeps natural words |
| S11 | One term per thing | Same |
| S12 | No noun stacks over three words | Same |
| S13 | One topic per paragraph, six sentences at most | Same |
| S14 | Procedure apart from description, warnings first | Same |
| S15 | Simple punctuation, no semicolons | Strict: also no contractions |

More examples: references/ste80-rules.md. Full strict rules and a checklist: references/strict-mode.md. More than 100 plain-word swaps: references/word-swaps.md.

## Checker

`scripts/ste_check.py` is a small Python linter with no dependencies. It flags many Pass 1 tells, such as not-X-but-Y, chatbot phrases, run-ups, fake depth, stacked hedges, vague authority and association, "-ing" riders, inflated claims, AI words, hyphen pairs and curly quotes. It also flags the measurable Pass 2 rules: sentence and paragraph length, semicolons, dashes, passive voice, perfect and progressive tenses, "-ing" forms and phrasal verbs.

```bash
python scripts/ste_check.py README.md
python scripts/ste_check.py --strict docs/runbook.md
cat draft.txt | python scripts/ste_check.py -
```

It is a heuristic, not an AI detector and not a compliance checker.

## Tests

`evals/` has four cases in the `claude plugin eval` format: a README rewrite, an explanation from scratch, a strict runbook and a casual LinkedIn post that does not mention STE. Run them with `claude plugin eval . --allow-tools Write,Edit,Bash`.

What we saw: when the prompt names ASD-STE100, the base model already gets the style mostly right. The skill made the difference in fidelity. In the LinkedIn rewrite, the run without the skill invented a quote and changed "40+ customers" to "40-odd". The run with the skill kept every fact. In the README rewrite, it kept "you may need to" and flagged a contradiction in the source. These are small tests, so treat them as a hint, not proof.

## Limits

- **STE is for clear explanatory text.** For fiction, speeches and brand copy, the skill does Pass 1 only.
- **STE is an English standard.** For other languages, the skill applies the tells and the structure rules, but not the English word lists.
- **"STE style" is not "STE compliant."** Compliance needs the official dictionary, trained writers and review.

## Sources and credits

- Andrej Karpathy on X, 2 October 2026: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479

- blader/humanizer by Siqi Chen (MIT). Pass 1 follows its 26-pattern catalog and order, with new examples. Its license notice is in LICENSE.

## Disclaimer

This skill does not contain the ASD-STE100 specification or its dictionary. The STE rules are paraphrased and simplified. ASD-STE100 and Simplified Technical English are trademarks of ASD (AeroSpace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe). This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by ASD.

title: Show HN: Face analysis tools with on-device photo processing
author: monstro_yu
body:
Face Analysis Tools 
 Attractiveness test 
 Full Face Report 
 FAQs 
Face Analysis
 AI face analysis, free and private
 Explore your facial features with tools for attractiveness, face shape and symmetry. Start with a free face score. Your photo stays on-device.
 Try the free attractiveness test No sign-up to scan. No photo upload to our servers.
 Explore face analysis tools
 Free · Available now Attractiveness test
 Get a free 0–100 photo geometry score and your strongest feature.
 Free · Available now Face symmetry test
 Explore how left and right facial landmarks align.
 Free · Available now Golden ratio face test
 Explore facial proportions without treating a ratio as a beauty rule.
 Free · Available now Jawline analysis
 Learn about lower-face proportions and how pose affects them.
 Free · Available now Canthal tilt test
 Explore eye-corner angles and the limits of photo measurements.
 Free · Available now Face shape test
 Explore face outline and proportions for styling inspiration.
How it works
 Start with one clear, front-facing photograph. Include your forehead, both cheeks and your chin, keep the camera centered, and relax your expression. Choose a JPG, PNG or WebP image up to 10 MB. You can select the file immediately; analysis begins when the browser is ready. The first scan downloads the landmark model, so it can take longer than later attempts. You do not need an account to try the free tools.
 Next, your browser locates facial landmarks and calculates a photo geometry score from 0 to 100. The free attractiveness result also names the strongest of three measured alignment groups. The example below uses fictional measurements to show the presentation. It is not a real person's result or a promise about your own score. Lighting, expression and camera position can affect the estimate.
 Finally, decide whether the explanations would be useful. You can keep exploring the free tools or sign in to purchase a Full Face Report. Review the complete sample before paying. Buying a report unlocks detail; it does not change your free score or make the photograph more accurate.
 DEMO · Screenshot of our sample result, using fictional measurements. What we measure
 The Full Face Report contains 30 distances and 12 paired landmark differences. Distances are expressed relative to cheek-to-cheek face width, so they describe proportions in the photograph rather than millimeters. These six groups organize the measurements and link to the free tools that help explain their context.
 Eyes and brows 
 Eye widths, openings, spacing and brow spans describe the eye area. The canthal tilt tool separately explains the angle between eye corners; width and tilt answer different questions.
Jaw and lower face 
 Jaw width, chin taper and lower-face height describe the visible lower outline. Read about projected outline angles and why they cannot establish the anatomical angle of a jaw bone.
Vertical proportions 
 Overall height and upper, middle and lower segments show how selected lengths relate. The ratio calculator compares three explicit ratios with phi without treating that number as a beauty target.
Paired alignment 
 Twelve pairs cover eyes, brows, nose wings, mouth corners, cheeks, jaw corners and chin edges. Their differences depend on the estimated midline and the photographed pose.
Face outline 
 Forehead, temple, jaw and chin widths help describe the outline. Shape labels are approximate styling categories, so read the measurements alongside the category rather than treating it as a fixed identity.
Nose and mouth proportions 
 Nose width, mouth width, lip distances and nearby spacing add detail to the central face. Expression changes these measurements; the mouth-to-nose comparison is especially sensitive to a smile.
Free score vs Full Face Report
 The free score gives you a quick introduction to the geometry of one photograph. You can see the overall alignment summary and strongest feature without creating an account. The five focused tools also remain free, so you can explore eye tilt, symmetry, proportions, jaw outline and face shape before deciding whether to buy anything.
 Free and paid face analysis features Feature Free score Full Face Report 
 Score and strongest feature Included Included 
 42 explained measurements Not included Included 
 Styling plan and PDF Not included Included 
 Account Not required Required 
 Payment Free One-time purchase 
A Full Face Report explains each measurement, suggests reversible styling experiments and provides a downloadable PDF. An account ties the purchased report to its owner. Paying adds explanations and access to the report; it does not buy a higher score or a more flattering interpretation. The same measurement limits apply to free and paid results, including sensitivity to camera position and expression.
 Explore the sample Full Face Report to see the actual layout and all 42 explanations. Then visit pricing for current purchase options and refund conditions. Start with the information you need rather than assuming that a paid result is necessary for everyone.
 Why on-device
 A portrait is personal. Our image analysis runs inside your browser, so choosing a photo does not send its image bytes to our servers. The browser downloads the detection software and model, reads the image locally and calculates numerical measurements. Those downloads are network requests for software, not uploads of your photograph. We do not use your selected image to train a model.
 Local processing does not mean every part of the website operates offline. Page assets, analytics, account access and payment services still use network connections. The attractiveness tool may retain numerical scan values in your browser session so you can sign in and continue to checkout. When you purchase a report, numerical measurements and order information are saved to your account to deliver it. Your original photograph is not part of that saved report.
 This distinction helps you decide what to share. You can try the free experience before providing account or payment information, and you can inspect the sample report without choosing any photo at all. Use a device and browser session you trust, especially on a shared computer. Our privacy policy explains account information and service providers; the About page describes our method and its limits.
Face analysis FAQs
 Is face analysis free?
 Yes. The attractiveness test gives you a free 0–100 photo geometry score and your strongest feature without signing up. You can also use the focused tools for free. A Full Face Report is optional and adds explained measurements, styling ideas and a PDF through a one-time purchase.
Is my photo uploaded?
 No. Facial landmark detection runs in your browser, and your original photo stays on your device. Buying a report saves numerical measurements and order details, not your image. The site still downloads software and uses network connections for account access, analytics and payments; local photo processing does not mean the whole site is offline.
What does my face score mean?
 It is a heuristic estimate based on landmark alignment in one photo, not a scientific measure of beauty or personal worth. Pose, lighting and expression can change the result. A higher number is not a promise of how other people perceive you, and the score should not guide medical decisions.
Which tools can I use today?
 All six core tools are live: attractiveness, symmetry, golden ratio, jawline, canthal tilt and face shape. Each provides free local photo analysis without sign-up. Choose the tool that answers your specific question, read its measurement explanation, and use comparable photos if you want to check whether a result repeats.

title: Show HN: Every satellite that passed over any place this week, and its photos
author: a585gupt
body:
hey HN, i built this because i wanted to know what had actually photographed my street.type in any place and it finds every satellite that passed over it in the last 7 days (SGP4 on the CelesTrak catalog, runs in your browser in about half a second), then pulls the real Sentinel-2 / Landsat / NASA images from those passes.some fun bits:
- the pass search can't skip a pass. checked it against a brute force on poles, the antimeridian and tiny swaths: 0 missed
- all ~17k objects in orbit are drawn on the GPU, solving Kepler's equation every frame
- Sentinel-2 timestamps are often 5-10 min off from when the sat actually crosses your spot, which was a fun one to figure outit only says "watched" if a real image exists, and it doesn't store your location.code: https://github.com/dev-Armaan/satelliteswould love feedback, especially on what data sources to add

title: Show HN: A doc server where Claude or local agent edits based on added comments
author: smarch27
body:
~/ smarchone/docs
Star on GitHub 
Comment on your docs.
 Claude makes the edits. 
tl;dr Comment on your repo's Markdown docs in the browser. Claude Code, or any local agent, edits the file and replies.
The problem 
Editing a doc from the terminal means describing where the problem is: "second section, the bullet about retries…"
Then you scroll a diff to check it got the right spot.
That's a lot of attention for a one-line fix, and you lose your place in the doc.
How it works
One small daemon on your machine. Each repo's agent connects to it with a skill and a polling script.
Browser 
 The editor
One tab for every repo. You read, highlight and comment. Changes stream in live.
⇄ comments
edits
Daemon 
 docs serve · localhost:3459
Owns the workspaces. Stores each doc's comment threads and version history, and queues threads as jobs for that repo's agent.
repo-a/.docs threads · history · job queue 
repo-b/.docs threads · history · job queue 
⇄ jobs
replies
Agent, per repo 
 Skill + poll.sh 
Claude Code with the /collab-docs skill, or any local agent. It edits the Markdown file directly and posts replies.
The skill registers the current repo as a workspace. docs serve "$PWD" starts the daemon if needed. 
The polling script waits on the daemon in the background. It's a long-poll, so an idle agent uses no tokens. 
When you comment, the daemon hands the page's threads to that repo's agent and locks the page. The agent edits the file, replies, and the page unlocks. 
GitHub → 
See it work
Two comments on a spec. One asks for an edit, the other asks a question. You never leave the page.
Docs — specs/retries.md
skip ⏭ 
Claude is listening 
Retries
.docs/specs/retries.md
When a request to the upstream API fails, the client should, in most cases and depending on the type of error that was returned, consider trying the request again a number of times before eventually giving up. 
Backoff
Waits double after each attempt, starting at 200 ms, with a little jitter so clients don't retry in lockstep.
We give up after 5 attempts. Errors after that go to the dead-letter queue.
Comments 
Get started in 1 minute
npm i -g @smarchone/docs Node 22+ copy 
npx skills add smarchone/docs --skill collab-docs -g copy 
/collab-docs in Claude Code, in any repo copy 
Then open http://127.0.0.1:3459 and leave your first comment. Or skip the global install: npx @smarchone/docs serve
space to skip · runs on your machine, nothing leaves it

Explore, Compare, Visualize datasets online
 Slicelytics is an online tool for exploring, comparing, and charting JSON, NDJSON/JSONL, CSV, TOON, and FIT datasets. Built for developers, data scientists, and analysts - no setup, no code, and your data never leaves your browser. 
 Launch Now 
 Experience the Workflow
 Try our fully functional demo below to get a feel for our product.

0: Object {...}

 Get Started ...or watch the walkthrough
 Let us walk you through the basics of Slicelytics features.
Built for Modern Data Professionals
 Our aim is to provide a no-nonsense alternative for individuals and smaller teams who are serious about data quality. All our tools are fully self-service, provided at a fair flat price, with no lock-in, no demos, no sales calls... 
 Data Exploration
 Slicelytics provides tools to understand your JSON, NDJSON/JSONL, CSV, TOON, and FIT datasets. Our powerful filtering takes you way beyond what a generic json formatter can do. 
 Our engine automatically infers schemas and maps data types across deeply nested structures of arbitrary depth. Filter by property name or by value (e.g. status="error" or level!="debug" ), with autocomplete for nested properties and every active filter shown as a chip you can remove in one click. 
 Dealing with high-volume or compressed data? We natively support Gzip and Zstandard decompression right in your browser, ensuring your workflow remains local and private. 
 Learn More 
Structural Diffing at Scale
 Standard diff tools fail on rich, structured data. Our comparison engine is built for hierarchy, allowing you to track changes across multiple dataset versions side-by-side. 
 Isolate deltas with intelligent filters that automatically adapt to your data's schema. Identify modifications in even the largest arrays and nested objects effortlessly. Both datasets can be large NDJSON files, streamed and loaded side by side, batch by batch. 
 See the evolution of your state: track both original and updated values for every property and array item with clear, high-contrast highlighting. Share a diff as a single link that carries both datasets. 
 Learn More 
Zero-Config Data Visualization
 Transform tabular and nested data into compelling stories with no code required. Bridge the gap between raw logs and actionable intelligence. 
 Calculate critical statistical metrics—mean, median, mode, standard deviation, variance, and more—and plot them instantly. Numbers and ISO 8601 dates are both supported. 
 Choose from a comprehensive suite of performance-optimized visualizations: bar charts, line charts, scatter plots, histograms, bubble charts, radar maps, and beyond. Only your data sets the limit. 
 Learn More 
Share Data with a Link
 Send a colleague exactly what you see. Click Share to copy a link that opens the same page, properties, filters, and chart, with the data as you filtered it. On Compare, one link carries both datasets. They don't need an account to open it. 
 The data is compressed into the part of the link after # , which browsers never send to a server. Nothing is uploaded, and nothing is stored by us. 
 Links suit small and medium datasets, as browsers limit how long a link can be (about 2 MB in Chrome). Hide what your colleague doesn't need before sharing, and the link gets shorter. 
 Learn More 
Open Data from AI Agents
 AI coding agents such as Claude Code can open your datasets in Slicelytics for you. Ask your agent to "chart p95 latency per day from runs.csv", and Slicelytics opens with the right page, properties, filters, and chart already set up. 
 For small and medium datasets, your agent builds a link. The data travels in the part of the link after # , which browsers never send to a server. 
 For larger datasets, watch a folder: links have size limits, files in a folder don't. Your agent writes each dataset into a folder on your computer, and new files show up in Slicelytics automatically. Available in Chrome and Edge. 
 Learn More 
What's New in Slicelytics
 Recent features and improvements, updated October 21, 2026 . 
 Oct 2026 Hover any change in Compare to find it in both datasets
 Hover a change in the Diff view to highlight that exact value in both datasets, however deeply nested.
Oct 2026 FIT files in links
 Agents can now open FIT files with a link, not only through a watched folder.
Oct 2026 Pick items by index in "Filters"
 Type e.g. [0-100] or [1,5,10] in "Filters" to show only those items.
Oct 2026 See how many items a dataset has, and how many are shown
 Explore and Compare now show how many items a dataset has, how many are shown, and how many have changes.
Oct 2026 Open FIT files from fitness devices
 Open FIT files from Garmin, Polar, Suunto and other devices in Explore, Compare and Visualize.
Oct 2026 Large CSV, TSV and JSON files load like NDJSON
 Large CSV, TSV and JSON files now stream in like NDJSON, showing the first 100 items straight away.
See the full changelog Frequently Asked Questions
 Who is Slicelytics for? Slicelytics is built for software engineers, data scientists, and analysts who need to inspect and debug structured data locally. It is a self-service utility tool for individuals and small teams. 
What use cases is Slicelytics built for? The core features are data exploration (filtering and traversing nested structures), structural diffing (comparing hierarchical data to identify additions, modifications, and deletions), and data visualization (generating charts and calculating statistical metrics without writing code). 
What file formats are supported? Slicelytics parses JSON, NDJSON/JSONL, CSV, TSV, and TOON files, and FIT files from Garmin, Polar, Suunto and other fitness devices, plain or compressed with Gzip (.gz) or Zstandard (.zst). 
Does Slicelytics work with compressed data? Yes. It includes native Gzip and Zstandard decompression implemented in the browser. Data is decompressed client-side without being sent to an external server. 
What limitations are there? Since data processing happens entirely in the browser, performance is constrained by your local machine's memory capacity and the JavaScript engine's limits. Large NDJSON files are streamed in the background, in Explore and on both sides of Compare, with experimental support for files of several gigabytes. Files in other formats are read into memory whole, then shown 100 items at a time. Shared links are compressed, but browsers limit how long a link can be (about 2 MB in Chrome), so sharing suits small and medium datasets. Watching a folder and installing Slicelytics as an app need Chrome or Edge. 
Can I use Slicelytics to collaborate with my colleagues? Yes, for small and medium datasets. Click the Share button in the bottom right corner to copy a link to what is on your screen: the data as filtered, plus the view (page, properties, filters, and chart settings). On Compare, the link carries both datasets. The data is compressed into the part of the link after # , which browsers never send to a server, so it is never stored by us. Your colleagues don't need an account or a subscription to open the link. 
Can I filter JSON data by a value? Yes. Type a value filter such as status="error" in the properties filter to keep only the items where that property has that value, or use != to leave them out instead: level!="debug" keeps everything else, items without a level included. Filters work on nested properties too: records.type="sleep" keeps the matching items and also removes the non-matching elements from the nested records array. 
Can AI agents like Claude Code open data in Slicelytics? Yes. An agent builds a Slicelytics link as described in slicelytics.com/llms.txt . The link opens Explore, Compare, or Visualize with your dataset and a ready-made view: which properties to show, value filters, the x-axis, and the chart type and metric. The data travels in the part of the link after # , so it is never sent to a server. 
Can Slicelytics show new files as a script writes them? Yes, in Chrome and Edge. Click "Watch a folder" in the Explore view and pick a folder on your computer. Slicelytics lists its JSON, NDJSON, CSV, TOON, and FIT files, and new files show up in the list as they are written; click one to load it. The folder is remembered across visits. 
Can I install Slicelytics as a desktop app? Yes, from Chrome or Edge. Installed, Slicelytics runs in its own window. Links you open go to the window you already have open, which offers them with a "Show" button instead of replacing what you are looking at. 
What visualisation options are available? Available chart types include bar, line, pie, doughnut, scatter, bubble, radar, and polar area charts, plus histograms of how often each value occurs. Our Visualize tool also computes standard statistical metrics such as sum, mean, median, mode, min, max, range, standard deviation, and variance from (parts of) the loaded data. ISO 8601 dates and date-times can be charted too, and nested arrays such as matrices are charted as one series per row, or narrowed to the rows you pick, e.g. mlModel.layers.weights[0] .

# Traccia

Production-ready distributed tracing for AI agents and LLM applications

Traccia is a lightweight, high-performance Python SDK for observability and tracing of AI agents, LLM applications, and complex distributed systems. Built on OpenTelemetry standards with specialized instrumentation for AI workloads.

Traccia is available on PyPI.

## ✨ Features

- 🔍 Automatic Instrumentation: Auto-patch OpenAI, Anthropic, requests, and HTTP libraries
- 🤖 Framework Integrations: Support for LangChain, CrewAI, and OpenAI Agents SDK
- 📊 LLM-Aware Tracing: Track tokens, costs, prompts, and completions automatically
- 📈 OpenTelemetry Metrics: Emit OTEL-compliant metrics for accurate cost/token tracking (independent of sampling)
- ⚡ Zero-Config Start: Simple `init()` call with automatic config discovery
- 🎯 Decorator-Based: Trace any function with `@observe` decorator
- 🔧 Multiple Exporters: OTLP (compatible with Grafana Tempo, Jaeger, Zipkin), Console, or File
- 🛡️ Production-Ready: Rate limiting, error handling, config validation, robust flushing
- 🛡️ Guardrail Detection: Passive, zero-overhead detection of guardrails in traces — explicit, provider-native, and heuristic
- 📝 Type-Safe: Full Pydantic validation for configuration
- 🚀 High Performance: Efficient batching, async support, minimal overhead
- 🔐 Secure: No secrets in logs, configurable data truncation

### Installation

```
pip install traccia
```

### Basic Usage

```
from traccia import init, observe

# Initialize (auto-loads from traccia.toml if present)
init()

# Trace any function
@observe()
def my_function(x, y):
    return x + y

# That's it! Traces are automatically created and exported
result = my_function(2, 3)
```

### With LLM Calls

```
from traccia import init, observe
from openai import OpenAI

init()  # Auto-patches OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

@observe(as_type="llm")
def generate_text(prompt: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Automatically tracks: model, tokens, cost, prompt, completion, latency
text = generate_text("Write a haiku about Python")
```

### LangChain

Create a callback handler and pass it to `config={"callbacks": [traccia_handler]}`. Install the optional extra: `pip install traccia[langchain]`.

```
from traccia import init
from traccia.integrations.langchain import CallbackHandler  # or TracciaCallbackHandler
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

init()

# Create Traccia handler (no args)
traccia_handler = CallbackHandler()

# Use with any LangChain runnable
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")
result = llm.invoke(
    "Tell me a joke",
    config={"callbacks": [traccia_handler]}
)
```

Spans for LLM/chat model runs are created automatically with the same attributes as direct OpenAI instrumentation (model, prompt, usage, cost).

Note: `pip install traccia[langchain]` installs traccia plus `langchain-core`; you need this extra to use the callback handler. If you already have `langchain-core` (e.g. from `langchain` or `langchain-openai`), base `pip install traccia` may be enough at runtime, but `traccia[langchain]` is the supported way to get a compatible dependency.

### OpenAI Agents SDK

Traccia automatically detects and instruments the OpenAI Agents SDK when installed. No extra code needed:

```
from traccia import init
from agents import Agent, Runner

init()  # Automatically enables Agents SDK tracing

agent = Agent(
    name="Assistant",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant"
)
result = Runner.run_sync(agent, "Write a haiku about recursion")
```

Configuration: Auto-enabled by default when `openai-agents` is installed. To disable:

```
init(openai_agents=False)  # Explicit parameter
# OR set environment variable: TRACCIA_OPENAI_AGENTS=false
# OR in traccia.toml under [instrumentation]: openai_agents = false
```

Compatibility: If you have `openai-agents` installed but don't use it (e.g., using LangChain or pure OpenAI instead), the integration is registered but never invoked—no overhead or extra spans.

### CrewAI

Traccia automatically instruments CrewAI when it is installed in your environment.

```
from traccia import init
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew, Process

init()  # Auto-enables CrewAI tracing when CrewAI is installed

researcher = Agent(role="Research Analyst", goal="Research a topic", llm="gpt-4o-mini")
task = Task(description="Research Shawn Michaels", agent=researcher)

crew = Crew(agents=[researcher], tasks=[task], process=Process.sequential, verbose=True)
result = crew.kickoff()
```

Traccia will create spans for the crew (`crewai.crew.kickoff`), each task (`crewai.task.*`), agents (`crewai.agent.*`), and underlying LLM calls, which nest under the existing OpenAI spans.

Configuration: Auto-enabled by default when `crewai` is installed. To disable:

```
init(crewai=False)  # Explicit parameter
# OR set environment variable: TRACCIA_CREWAI=false
# OR in traccia.toml under [instrumentation]: crewai = false
```

## 🛡️ Guardrail Detection

Traccia includes a passive guardrail detection engine that runs as a span processor — no runtime enforcement, no changes required to existing agent code. It inspects every span as it ends, classifies guardrail signals into structured findings, and writes results back onto spans so they appear in any configured exporter.

### How it works

Detection is automatic once `traccia.init()` is called. The processor runs three tiers against every span's attributes:

| Tier | Source | Confidence | How |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A — Explicit | `explicit` | `high` | `@observe(as_type="guardrail")` or `guardrail_span()` |
| B — Provider-native | `provider_native` | `high`/`medium` | LLM finish reason, stop reason, safety ratings |
| C — Heuristic | `heuristic` | always `low` | Denial keywords in tool error messages |

At the end of each trace (when the root span ends), the processor evaluates which guardrail categories should exist given the agent's observed capabilities (LLM calls, tool use, user-provided text) and reports which are missing.

### Annotating guardrails explicitly (Tier A)

Option 1: `guardrail_span` context manager — recommended for inline checks

```
from traccia.guardrails import guardrail_span

with guardrail_span("pii_check", category="pii", enforcement_mode="warn") as span:
    result = run_pii_check(user_input)
    span.set_attribute("guardrail.triggered", result.found_pii)
```

Option 2: `@observe(as_type="guardrail")` decorator — for function-level guardrails

If your guardrail function returns a `bool`, `guardrail.triggered` is set automatically:

```
from traccia import observe

@observe(
    as_type="guardrail",
    attributes={
        "guardrail.name": "prompt_injection_check",
        "guardrail.category": "prompt_injection",
        "guardrail.enforcement_mode": "block",
    }
)
def check_injection(text: str) -> bool:
    return any(kw in text.lower() for kw in INJECTION_KEYWORDS)
    # True → triggered (blocked), False → not triggered
```

For non-bool returns, set `guardrail.triggered` manually on the current span.

### Suppressing false positive missing-guardrail warnings

Batch pipelines or internal-only agents often get flagged for `prompt_injection` / `input_validation` because they make LLM calls with `llm.prompt`. Suppress specific categories for a run:

```
from traccia.guardrails import guardrail_span

# Convenience: suppress_missing on guardrail_span
with guardrail_span("root", category="unknown", suppress_missing=["prompt_injection", "input_validation"]):
    run_batch_pipeline()

# Or directly on any span
from traccia.guardrails import ATTR_GUARDRAIL_SUPPRESS_MISSING
span.set_attribute(ATTR_GUARDRAIL_SUPPRESS_MISSING, ["prompt_injection"])
```

### What appears in traces

Per span (when a guardrail signal is found):

- `guardrail.finding.count` — number of findings on this span
- `guardrail.findings` — JSON array of `GuardrailFinding` objects

On the root span (aggregated summary of the entire run):

- `guardrail.summary` — full `GuardrailSummary` JSON
- `guardrail.summary.coverage_confidence` — `"high"`, `"medium"`, or `"low"`
- `guardrail.summary.missing_count` — number of expected-but-missing guardrail categories
- `guardrail.summary.detected_categories` — list of detected category strings

### Provider-native detection (Tier B, automatic)

These signals are detected automatically from LLM span attributes — no annotation required:

| Provider | Signal | Attribute |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI | `finish_reason = "content_filter"` | `llm.finish_reason` |
| Azure OpenAI | `finish_reason = "content_filtered"` | `llm.finish_reason` |
| Google GenAI | `finish_reason = "SAFETY"` | `llm.finish_reason` |
| Anthropic | `stop_reason = "content_filter"` | `llm.stop_reason` |
| Anthropic | Policy violation error message | `error.message` + `llm.vendor=anthropic` |
| Google/LangChain | `"blocked": true` or `"probability": "HIGH"` in safety ratings | `llm.safety_ratings` |

### Disabling Tier C (heuristic) detection

Tier A/B stay on. Turn off tool-error keyword heuristics if you do not want Tier C at all:

```
init(guardrail_heuristics=False)
```

Or `TRACCIA_GUARDRAIL_HEURISTICS=false`, or in `traccia.toml`: `[instrumentation]` → `guardrail_heuristics = false`.

### Hard limits — what cannot be captured

- Guardrails running outside the traced process (API gateways, proxies, external validators) are invisible unless they write span attributes.
- A guardrail that exists but never fires cannot be distinguished from a missing guardrail. Only explicit annotation proves presence.
- Prompt injection detection requires an explicit span — the model's output alone cannot reliably indicate whether a check ran.
- Capability inference (`handles_user_text`) is inferred from `llm.prompt` being present; batch pipelines and user-facing agents look the same. Use suppression to opt out.

### Configuration Precedence

Traccia merges configuration from multiple sources with the following priority (highest to lowest):

1. Explicit parameters — `init(endpoint="...", agent_id="...")` or `start_tracing(...)`
2. Environment variables — `TRACCIA_ENDPOINT`, `TRACCIA_AGENT_ID`, etc.
3. Config file — `traccia.toml` (current directory) or `~/.traccia/config.toml`
4. Defaults — Built-in SDK defaults

Example: If you set `TRACCIA_ENDPOINT` in your environment and pass `endpoint=...` to `init()`, the explicit parameter wins.

### Configuration File

Create a `traccia.toml` file in your project root:

```
traccia config init
```

This creates a template config file:

```
[tracing]
# API key — required for the Traccia platform, not needed for local OTLP backends
api_key = ""

# Endpoint URL for OTLP trace ingestion (default: Traccia platform)
# For local OTLP backends use e.g. endpoint = "http://localhost:4318/v1/traces"
endpoint = "https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces"

sample_rate = 1.0           # 0.0 to 1.0
auto_start_trace = true     # Auto-start root trace on init
auto_trace_name = "root"    # Name for auto-started trace
use_otlp = true             # Use OTLP exporter
# service_name = "my-app"   # Optional service name
# service_role has no env var — pass via init(service_role="orchestrator")

[exporters]
# Only enable ONE exporter at a time
enable_console = false        # Print traces to console
enable_file = false           # Write traces to file
file_exporter_path = "traces.jsonl"
reset_trace_file = false      # Reset file on initialization

[instrumentation]
enable_patching = true          # Auto-patch libraries (OpenAI, Anthropic, requests)
enable_token_counting = true    # Count tokens for LLM calls
enable_costs = true             # Calculate costs
openai_agents = true            # Auto-enable OpenAI Agents SDK integration
crewai = true                   # Auto-enable CrewAI integration
guardrail_heuristics = true     # Tier C heuristic guardrail detection (tool error keywords)
auto_instrument_tools = false   # Auto-instrument tool calls (experimental)
max_tool_spans = 100            # Max tool spans to create
max_span_depth = 10             # Max nested span depth

[rate_limiting]
# Optional: limit spans per second
# max_spans_per_second = 100.0
max_queue_size = 5000           # Max buffered spans
max_block_ms = 100              # Max ms to block before dropping
max_export_batch_size = 512     # Spans per export batch
schedule_delay_millis = 5000    # Delay between batches

[metrics]
enable_metrics = true           # Enable OpenTelemetry metrics
# metrics_endpoint = ""         # Defaults to {traces_base}/v2/metrics
metrics_sample_rate = 1.0       # Metrics sampling rate (1.0 = 100%)

[runtime]
# Optional runtime metadata (agent identity: prefer init(agent_id=..., agent_name=..., env=...) or TRACCIA_* env)
# session_id = ""
# user_id = ""
# tenant_id = ""
# project_id = ""
# agent_id = ""   # Single-agent: set in code or TRACCIA_AGENT_ID
# agent_name = ""
# env = ""        # e.g. production, staging, dev

[logging]
debug = false                   # Enable debug logging
enable_span_logging = false     # Enable span-level logging

[advanced]
# attr_truncation_limit = 1000  # Max attribute value length
```

### Default endpoint

If you do not set `endpoint` (in config, environment, or when calling `init()` / `start_tracing()`), the SDK uses the Traccia platform by default (`https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces`). You can override it to send traces to your own OTLP-compatible backend.

The default is defined in `traccia.config`: `DEFAULT_OTLP_TRACE_ENDPOINT`. The alias `DEFAULT_ENDPOINT` is kept for backward compatibility (same value).

### OTLP Backend Compatibility

Traccia is fully OTLP-compatible and works with:

- Grafana Tempo - `http://tempo:4318/v1/traces`
- Jaeger - `http://jaeger:4318/v1/traces`
- Zipkin - Configure via OTLP endpoint
- SigNoz - Self-hosted observability platform
- Traccia Platform - `https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces` (requires API key)

### Environment Variables

All config parameters can be set via environment variables with the `TRACCIA_` prefix:

Tracing: `TRACCIA_API_KEY`, `TRACCIA_ENDPOINT`, `TRACCIA_SAMPLE_RATE`, `TRACCIA_AUTO_START_TRACE`, `TRACCIA_AUTO_TRACE_NAME`, `TRACCIA_USE_OTLP`, `TRACCIA_SERVICE_NAME`

Exporters: `TRACCIA_ENABLE_CONSOLE`, `TRACCIA_ENABLE_FILE`, `TRACCIA_FILE_PATH`, `TRACCIA_RESET_TRACE_FILE`

Instrumentation: `TRACCIA_ENABLE_PATCHING`, `TRACCIA_ENABLE_TOKEN_COUNTING`, `TRACCIA_ENABLE_COSTS`, `TRACCIA_AUTO_INSTRUMENT_TOOLS`, `TRACCIA_MAX_TOOL_SPANS`, `TRACCIA_MAX_SPAN_DEPTH`, `TRACCIA_OPENAI_AGENTS`, `TRACCIA_CREWAI`, `TRACCIA_GUARDRAIL_HEURISTICS`

Rate Limiting: `TRACCIA_MAX_SPANS_PER_SECOND`, `TRACCIA_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE`, `TRACCIA_MAX_BLOCK_MS`, `TRACCIA_MAX_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE`, `TRACCIA_SCHEDULE_DELAY_MILLIS`

Runtime: `TRACCIA_SESSION_ID`, `TRACCIA_USER_ID`, `TRACCIA_TENANT_ID`, `TRACCIA_PROJECT_ID`, `TRACCIA_AGENT_ID`, `TRACCIA_AGENT_NAME`, `TRACCIA_ENV`

Legacy alias: `TRACCIA_PROJECT` (maps to `project_id`)

Logging: `TRACCIA_DEBUG`, `TRACCIA_ENABLE_SPAN_LOGGING`

Advanced: `TRACCIA_ATTR_TRUNCATION_LIMIT`

### Programmatic Configuration

```
from traccia import init

# Override config programmatically (including agent identity for single-agent services)
init(
    endpoint="http://tempo:4318/v1/traces",
    sample_rate=0.5,
    enable_costs=True,
    max_spans_per_second=100.0,
    agent_id="my-agent",
    agent_name="My Agent",
    env="production",
)
```

### Multi-Agent Orchestrator Services

For services that orchestrate many logical agents in one process, set a service role and scope per-run identity:

```
from traccia import init, runtime_config

init(
    service_name="my-multi-agent-api",
    service_role="orchestrator",
    auto_start_trace=False,
)

with runtime_config.run_identity(agent_id="billing-agent", agent_name="Billing Agent", env="production"):
    # run one logical agent task
    ...
```

This prevents the host service from being registered as a synthetic agent in the Traccia platform.

### Safe Parallel Runs in One Process

If one process runs many agents concurrently (for example, an API server or orchestrator), use this pattern:

- Call `init()` once per process (for example at startup), not per request.
- Wrap each logical "run" in `runtime_config.run_identity(...)` to set agent id/name/env for that run.
- Do not call `stop_tracing()` per request; use `force_flush()` to flush spans/metrics after a run without shutting down the provider.

```
from traccia import init, span, force_flush, runtime_config

init(service_name="multi-agent-service", auto_start_trace=False)

def run_agent(agent_id: str, env: str, payload: dict):
    # Scope identity to this run only
    with runtime_config.run_identity(agent_id=agent_id, agent_name=agent_id, env=env):
        with span("agent.run") as root:
            root.set_attribute("agent.id", agent_id)
            root.set_attribute("agent.run.mode", "api")
            # ... your agent logic here ...

    # Flush without tearing down the global provider
    force_flush(5.0)
```

### The `@observe` Decorator

The `@observe` decorator is the primary way to instrument your code:

```
from traccia import observe

# Basic usage
@observe()
def process_data(data):
    return transform(data)

# Custom span name
@observe(name="data_pipeline")
def process_data(data):
    return transform(data)

# Add custom attributes
@observe(attributes={"version": "2.0", "env": "prod"})
def process_data(data):
    return transform(data)

# Specify span type
@observe(as_type="llm")  # "span", "llm", "tool"
def call_llm():
    pass

# Skip capturing specific arguments
@observe(skip_args=["password", "secret"])
def authenticate(username, password):
    pass

# Skip capturing result (for large returns)
@observe(skip_result=True)
def fetch_large_dataset():
    return huge_data
```

Available Parameters:

- `name` (str, optional): Custom span name (defaults to function name)
- `attributes` (dict, optional): Initial span attributes
- `as_type` (str): Span type - `"span"`, `"llm"`, `"tool"`, or `"guardrail"`
- `skip_args` (list, optional): List of argument names to skip capturing
- `skip_result` (bool): Skip capturing the return value

### Async Functions

`@observe` works seamlessly with async functions:

```
@observe()
async def async_task(x):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return x * 2

result = await async_task(5)
```

### Manual Span Creation

For more control, create spans manually:

```
from traccia import get_tracer, span

# Using convenience function
with span("operation_name") as s:
    s.set_attribute("key", "value")
    s.add_event("checkpoint_reached")
    do_work()

# Using tracer directly
tracer = get_tracer("my_service")
with tracer.start_as_current_span("operation") as s:
    s.set_attribute("user_id", 123)
    do_work()
```

### Error Handling

Traccia automatically captures and records errors:

```
@observe()
def failing_function():
    raise ValueError("Something went wrong")

# Span will contain:
# - error.type: "ValueError"
# - error.message: "Something went wrong"
# - error.stack_trace: (truncated stack trace)
# - span status: ERROR
```

### Nested Spans

Spans are automatically nested based on call hierarchy:

```
@observe()
def parent_operation():
    child_operation()
    return "done"

@observe()
def child_operation():
    grandchild_operation()

@observe()
def grandchild_operation():
    pass

# Creates nested span hierarchy:
# parent_operation
#   └── child_operation
#       └── grandchild_operation
```

## 🛠️ CLI Tools

Traccia includes a powerful CLI for configuration and diagnostics:

### `traccia config init`

Create a new `traccia.toml` configuration file:

```
traccia config init
traccia config init --force  # Overwrite existing
```

### `traccia doctor`

Validate configuration and diagnose issues:

```
traccia doctor

# Output:
# 🩺 Running Traccia configuration diagnostics...
# 
# ✅ Found config file: ./traccia.toml
# ✅ Configuration is valid
# 
# 📊 Configuration summary:
#    • API Key: ❌ Not set (optional)
#    • Endpoint: https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces
#    • Sample Rate: 1.0
#    • OTLP Exporter: ✅ Enabled
```

### `traccia check`

Test connectivity to your exporter endpoint:

```
traccia check
traccia check --endpoint http://tempo:4318/v1/traces
```

### Rate Limiting

Protect your infrastructure with built-in rate limiting:

```
[rate_limiting]
max_spans_per_second = 100.0  # Limit to 100 spans/sec
max_queue_size = 5000         # Max buffered spans
max_block_ms = 100             # Block up to 100ms before dropping
```

Behavior:

1. Try to acquire capacity immediately
2. If unavailable, block for up to `max_block_ms`
3. If still unavailable, drop span and log warning

When spans are dropped due to rate limiting, warnings are logged to help you monitor and adjust limits.

### Sampling

Control trace volume with sampling:

```
# Sample 10% of traces
init(sample_rate=0.1)

# Sampling is applied at trace creation time
# Traces are either fully included or fully excluded
```

### Token Counting & Cost Calculation

Automatic for supported LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic):

```
@observe(as_type="llm")
def call_openai(prompt):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Span automatically includes:
# - llm.token.prompt_tokens
# - llm.token.completion_tokens
# - llm.token.total_tokens
# - llm.cost.total (in USD)
```

### Metrics

Traccia emits OTEL-compliant metrics for accurate cost and token tracking, independent of trace sampling.

#### Why Metrics?

With trace sampling (e.g., `sample_rate=0.1`), only 10% of traces are exported. Cost calculated from traces will be 10x underestimated. Metrics solve this by recording data for every LLM call, regardless of sampling.

#### Default Metrics

Traccia automatically emits these metrics:

| Metric | Type | Unit | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gen_ai.client.token.usage` | Histogram | `{token}` | Input/output tokens per call |
| `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` | Histogram | `s` | LLM operation duration |
| `gen_ai.client.operation.cost` | Histogram | `usd` | Cost per call (USD) |
| `gen_ai.client.completions.exceptions` | Counter | `1` | Exception count |
| `gen_ai.agent.runs` | Counter | `1` | Agent runs (CrewAI, OpenAI Agents) |
| `gen_ai.agent.turns` | Counter | `1` | Agent turns |
| `gen_ai.agent.execution_time` | Histogram | `s` | Agent execution time |

Attributes: `gen_ai.system` (openai, anthropic), `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.agent.id`, `gen_ai.agent.name`

#### Configuration

```
from traccia import init

init(
    enable_metrics=True,  # Default: True
    metrics_endpoint="https://your-backend.com/v2/metrics",  
    metrics_sample_rate=1.0,  # Default: 1.0 (100%)
)
```

Or via `traccia.toml`:

```
[metrics]
enable_metrics = true
metrics_endpoint = "https://your-backend.com/v2/metrics"
metrics_sample_rate = 1.0
```

Or via environment variables:

```
export TRACCIA_ENABLE_METRICS=true
export TRACCIA_METRICS_ENDPOINT=https://your-backend.com/v2/metrics
export TRACCIA_METRICS_SAMPLE_RATE=1.0
```

#### Custom Metrics

Record your own metrics:

```
from traccia.metrics import record_counter, record_histogram

# Record a counter
record_counter("my_custom_events", 1, {"event_type": "user_action"})

# Record a histogram
record_histogram("my_custom_latency", 0.123, {"service": "api"}, unit="s")
```

#### Agent Metrics vs. Plain LLM Calls

Agent-level metrics (such as `gen_ai.agent.runs` and `gen_ai.agent.execution_time`) are only emitted when Traccia can see a real agent lifecycle (for example, CrewAI crews or OpenAI Agents SDK runs). For plain OpenAI/Anthropic calls and most simple LangChain usages, you will still get full LLM metrics (`gen_ai.client.*`), but no agent metrics unless you build an explicit agent abstraction on top.

### Enable Debug Logging

```
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

# Or via config
init(debug=True)

# Or via env var
# TRACCIA_DEBUG=1 python your_script.py
```

#### Traces not appearing

1. Check connectivity: `traccia check`
2. Validate config: `traccia doctor`
3. Enable debug logging
4. Verify endpoint is correct and accessible

#### High memory usage

- Reduce `max_queue_size` in rate limiting config
- Lower `sample_rate` to reduce volume
- Enable rate limiting with `max_spans_per_second`

#### Spans being dropped

- Check rate limiter logs for warnings
- Increase `max_spans_per_second` if set
- Increase `max_queue_size` if spans are queued
- Check `traccia doctor` output

#### `init(**kwargs) -> TracerProvider`

Initialize the Traccia SDK. All parameters are optional; configuration is merged from `traccia.toml` → env vars → explicit parameters (highest wins).

- `endpoint` (str): OTLP endpoint URL (default: `https://api.traccia.ai/v2/traces`)
- `api_key` (str): API key for the Traccia platform
- `sample_rate` (float): Sampling rate 0.0–1.0 (default: 1.0)
- `auto_start_trace` (bool): Auto-start a root trace on init (default: True)
- `auto_trace_name` (str): Name for the auto-started trace (default: `"root"`)
- `use_otlp` (bool): Use OTLP exporter (default: True)
- `service_name` (str): Service name (auto-detected if not set)
- `service_role` (str): `"orchestrator"` to prevent this service being registered as an agent
- `config_file` (str): Path to a custom `traccia.toml`

- `enable_console_exporter` (bool): Print spans to stdout (default: False)
- `enable_file_exporter` (bool): Write spans to file (default: False)
- `file_exporter_path` (str): Path for file exporter (default: `"traces.jsonl"`)
- `reset_trace_file` (bool): Clear file on init (default: False)

- `enable_patching` (bool): Auto-patch OpenAI, Anthropic, requests (default: True)
- `enable_token_counting` (bool): Count tokens (default: True)
- `enable_costs` (bool): Calculate costs (default: True)
- `openai_agents` (bool): Auto-enable OpenAI Agents SDK integration (default: True)
- `crewai` (bool): Auto-enable CrewAI integration (default: True)
- `guardrail_heuristics` (bool): Enable Tier C heuristic guardrail detection (default: True)
- `auto_instrument_tools` (bool): Experimental tool auto-instrumentation (default: False)
- `max_tool_spans` (int): Max tool spans per trace (default: 100)
- `max_span_depth` (int): Max nested span depth (default: 10)

Agent identity (single-agent services)

- `agent_id` (str): Logical agent identifier
- `agent_name` (str): Human-readable agent name
- `env` (str): Deployment environment, e.g. `"production"`, `"staging"`

- `session_id` (str): Session identifier
- `user_id` (str): User identifier
- `tenant_id` (str): Tenant / org identifier
- `project_id` (str): Project identifier

- `enable_metrics` (bool): Emit OTEL metrics (default: True)
- `metrics_endpoint` (str): Metrics endpoint (derived from tracing endpoint if not set)
- `metrics_sample_rate` (float): Metrics sampling rate (default: 1.0)

Rate limiting

- `max_spans_per_second` (float): Rate limit spans/sec (default: None = unlimited)
- `max_block_ms` (int): Max ms to block before dropping a span (default: 100)
- `max_queue_size` (int): Max buffered spans (default: 5000)
- `max_export_batch_size` (int): Spans per export batch (default: 512)
- `schedule_delay_millis` (int): Batch export interval ms (default: 5000)

- `debug` (bool): Enable debug logging (default: False)
- `attr_truncation_limit` (int): Max attribute value length (default: None)

#### `stop_tracing(flush_timeout: float = 1.0) -> None`

Stop tracing and flush pending spans.

- `flush_timeout` (float): Max seconds to wait for flush

#### `get_tracer(name: str = "default") -> Tracer`

Get a tracer instance.

- `name` (str): Tracer name (typically module/service name)

#### `span(name: str, attributes: dict = None) -> Span`

Create a span context manager.

- `name` (str): Span name
- `attributes` (dict, optional): Initial attributes

Returns: Span context manager

#### `@observe(name=None, *, attributes=None, tags=None, as_type="span", skip_args=None, skip_result=False)`

Decorate a function to create spans automatically.

- `name` (str, optional): Span name (default: function name)
- `attributes` (dict, optional): Initial attributes
- `tags` (list[str], optional): User-defined identifiers for the observed method
- `as_type` (str): Span type (`"span"`, `"llm"`, `"tool"`, `"guardrail"`)
- `skip_args` (list, optional): Arguments to skip capturing
- `skip_result` (bool): Skip capturing return value

#### `load_config(config_file=None, overrides=None) -> TracciaConfig`

Load and validate configuration.

- `config_file` (str, optional): Path to config file
- `overrides` (dict, optional): Override values

Returns: Validated TracciaConfig instance

Raises: `ConfigError` if invalid

#### `validate_config(config_file=None, overrides=None) -> tuple[bool, str, TracciaConfig | None]`

Validate configuration without loading.

Returns: Tuple of (is_valid, message, config_or_none)

### Data Flow

```
Application Code (@observe)
        ↓
   Span Creation
        ↓
   Processors (token counting, cost, enrichment)
        ↓
   Rate Limiter (optional)
        ↓
   Batch Processor (buffering)
        ↓
   Exporter (OTLP/Console/File)
        ↓
   Backend (Grafana Tempo / Jaeger / Zipkin / etc.)

```

### Instrumentation vs Integrations

- `traccia.instrumentation.*`: Infrastructure and vendor instrumentation.

- HTTP client/server helpers (including FastAPI middleware).
- Vendor SDK hooks and monkey patching (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, `requests`).
- Decorators and utilities used for auto-instrumenting arbitrary functions.
- `traccia.integrations.*`: AI/agent framework integrations.

- Adapters that plug into higher-level frameworks via their official extension points (e.g., LangChain callbacks).
- Work at the level of chains, tools, agents, and workflows rather than raw HTTP or SDK calls.

## 🤝 Contributing

Contributions are welcome! Whether it's bug fixes, new features, documentation improvements, or examples - we appreciate your help.

### How to Contribute

1. Fork the repository
2. Create a feature branch: `git checkout -b feature/amazing-feature`
3. Make your changes and add tests
4. Run tests: `pytest traccia/tests/`
5. Lint your code: `ruff check traccia/`
6. Commit: `git commit -m "Add amazing feature"`
7. Push: `git push origin feature/amazing-feature`
8. Open a Pull Request

### Development Setup

```
# Clone the repository (Python SDK)
git clone https://github.com/traccia-ai/traccia-py.git
cd traccia-py

# Create virtual environment
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate  # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate

# Install in editable mode with dev dependencies
pip install -e ".[dev]"

# Run tests
pytest traccia/tests/ -v

# Run with coverage
pytest traccia/tests/ --cov=traccia --cov-report=html
```

### Code Style

- Follow PEP 8
- Use type hints where appropriate
- Add docstrings for public APIs
- Write tests for new features
- Keep PRs focused and atomic

### Areas We'd Love Help With

- Integrations: Add support for more LLM providers (Cohere, AI21, local models)
- Backends: Test and document setup with different OTLP backends
- Examples: Real-world examples of agent instrumentation
- Documentation: Tutorials, guides, video walkthroughs
- Performance: Optimize hot paths, reduce overhead
- Testing: Improve test coverage, add integration tests

## 📄 License

Apache License 2.0 - see LICENSE for full terms and conditions.

## 🙏 Acknowledgments

Built with:

- OpenTelemetry - Vendor-neutral observability framework
- Pydantic - Data validation
- tiktoken - Token counting

Inspired by observability tools in the ecosystem and designed to work seamlessly with the OTLP standard.

## About

 OpenTelemetry-based tracing SDK for AI agents and LLM applications
